## Overview {#sec-flow-overview}

Flow matching is a method for training a generative model that maps a noise sample $X_0\sim p$, usually Gaussian, to a sample $X_1\sim q$ of the data distribution by solving an ordinary differential equation (ODE). A neural network $u_t^\theta$ represents the velocity field of this ODE. To train it, one first chooses a probability path $p_t$ from $p$ to $q$, for example the distribution of the points $X_t=(1-t)X_0+tX_1$ on straight lines between independent noise and data samples. The network should then match the velocity field that generates this path. This velocity field is not known, but the network can be regressed instead on the velocity $X_1-X_0$ of each straight line, which is known for every pair, because the two regressions have the same gradient. Training therefore needs no ODE solves, and after training a sample is generated by integrating the learned ODE from a noise sample at $t=0$ to $t=1$. The note consists of two parts.

**Part I. Flow matching.** Part I develops the method from its definitions. It starts with flows and their velocity fields (@sec-flow-fields) and then characterises, by the continuity equation, the velocity fields that generate a given probability path (@sec-ce). These results lead to the flow-matching and conditional flow-matching losses, whose gradients are shown to agree (@sec-fm). For Gaussian and affine conditional paths the training targets have closed forms, and Part I ends with these paths and a training example (@sec-gauss).

**Part II. Rectified flow and diffusion.** The straight-line path of this training example is the path of rectified flow, which is the subject of Part II. After a change of variables, the training objective of rectified flow and the denoising objective of a diffusion model differ only by a time weighting and have corresponding minimisers, so a rectified-flow velocity network and a diffusion denoiser can be converted into each other by an explicit formula (@sec-rf). @sec-flow-score then extends this correspondence to the affine Gaussian paths of @sec-affine by deriving the relations between velocity, score and denoiser, which hold where their coefficients are finite and nonzero.

## Flows and velocity fields {#sec-flow-fields}

### Why flow models? {#sec-flow-why}

Generation is the transport of a noise sample to a data sample by the ODE

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}X_t = u_t(X_t), \qquad X_0\sim p_0\ \text{(noise)}\ \longrightarrow\ X_1\sim p_1\ \text{(data)}.
$$ {#eq-transport}

Diffusion models and flow models both generate samples with an ODE of this form, but they learn different quantities. A diffusion model learns the score of a fixed noising SDE, and the ODE derived from it has curved trajectories, so an ODE solver needs many steps (@fig-paths, left). A flow model instead learns the velocity $u_t$ directly, for a path that is chosen in advance, for example a family of straight lines, and trajectories that are close to straight lines can be followed with few steps (@fig-paths, right). The straight lines are, however, the conditional paths of @sec-gauss, whereas the trajectories of the learned marginal velocity are in general not straight (@fig-lines, middle). The right panel therefore shows the case of exactly straight trajectories and not the typical trajectories of a model trained with these paths.

![Trajectories from noise samples (grey) to data samples (orange) for the probability-flow ODE of a diffusion model (left) and for a flow model with straight trajectories (right). The blue points on the trajectories mark solver steps, many on the left and few on the right. The diffusion trajectories are curved, so an ODE solver needs many steps to follow them, whereas the straight trajectories can be followed with few steps. Cropped from the lecture slides [@lecture-slides-flow].](figures/lec13/yws0322-slide05-curved-vs-straight.png){#fig-paths width=100%}

### Flows {#sec-flow-def}

The ODE @eq-transport describes the motion of one sample, and the solutions for all starting points together form the flow of the velocity field.

::: {#def-flow}
## Velocity field and flow
A velocity field is a map $u:[0,1]\times\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$, $(t,x)\mapsto u_t(x)$. A flow of $u$ is a map $\psi:[0,1]\times\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$, $(t,x)\mapsto\psi_t(x)$, that solves

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\psi_t(x)=u_t(\psi_t(x)),\qquad \psi_0(x)=x .
$$ {#eq-flow-ode}
:::

In words, $t\mapsto\psi_t(x)$ is the trajectory that starts at $x$ and has velocity $u_t$ at each time $t$. This trajectory is well defined only if the ODE has exactly one solution, and the standard condition for this is local Lipschitz continuity. The field $u$ is locally Lipschitz in $x$ if for every bounded set $K\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ there is a constant $L_K$ such that $\lVert u_t(x)-u_t(y)\rVert\le L_K\lVert x-y\rVert$ for all $x,y\in K$ and $t\in[0,1]$. Under this condition, if $u$ is continuous in $(t,x)$ and locally Lipschitz in $x$, then the Picard-Lindelof theorem gives, for every starting point $x$, exactly one solution of @eq-flow-ode on some interval $[0,t_x)$ [@lipman2024guide, Theorem 1]. Moreover, the theorem applies equally to the ODE started at any time $s$ from any point. Consequently, two trajectories that pass through the same point at some time $s$ solve the same initial value problem, so they coincide at all times, and trajectories never cross.

Local existence is not enough, because a solution can leave every bounded set before $t=1$. For example, $u(x)=x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is smooth, but the solution from $x=2$ is $\psi_t(2)=2/(1-2t)$, which tends to infinity as $t\to\tfrac12$, so $\psi_1(2)$ is not defined. A sufficient condition for solutions on all of $[0,1]$ is linear growth, $\lVert u_t(x)\rVert\le a+b\lVert x\rVert$ for all $t\in[0,1]$ and $x$, with constants $a,b\ge0$ that do not depend on $t$. To see why this suffices, note that integrating the ODE gives $\lVert\psi_t(x)\rVert\le\lVert x\rVert+\int_0^t\big(a+b\lVert\psi_s(x)\rVert\big)\,\mathrm{d}s$, and Gronwall's inequality then gives $\lVert\psi_t(x)\rVert\le(\lVert x\rVert+at)\,e^{bt}$. The trajectory therefore stays in a bounded set, and a solution that stays bounded can be continued up to $t=1$. In addition, a velocity field with bounded first derivatives in $x$ is globally Lipschitz and therefore has linear growth. The same bound holds for the ODE run backwards in time, which is used below. The rest of this subsection therefore assumes that for every starting point the solutions exist on all of $[0,1]$ in both directions, which holds for example under linear growth.

Under these assumptions each $\psi_t$ is a bijection of $\mathbb{R}^d$. It is injective, because two different starting points with $\psi_t(x)=\psi_t(y)$ would give two trajectories that meet at time $t$, which the uniqueness above excludes. It is also surjective, with an explicit inverse, because for every $y$ the ODE can be solved backwards in time from the value $y$ at time $t$, and the value of this solution at time $0$ is $\psi_t^{-1}(y)$. Differentiability requires one more condition. If the derivative $\partial_xu_t(x)$ is continuous in $(t,x)$, then $\psi_t(x)$ is continuously differentiable in $x$ (differentiable dependence on initial data), and its Jacobian matrix $\partial_x\psi_t(x)$, with entries $[\partial_x\psi_t(x)]_{ij}=\partial[\psi_t(x)]_i/\partial x_j$, solves a linear ODE,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\partial_x\psi_t(x)&=\partial_xu_t\big(\psi_t(x)\big)\,\partial_x\psi_t(x),\qquad \partial_x\psi_0(x)=I,\\
\det\partial_x\psi_t(x)&=\exp\Big(\int_0^t\operatorname{div}u_s\big(\psi_s(x)\big)\,\mathrm{d}s\Big)>0 .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-jacobian}

The first equation follows by differentiating @eq-flow-ode in $x$. The determinant formula (Liouville's formula) then follows from $\tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\det\partial_x\psi_t(x)=\operatorname{tr}\big(\partial_xu_t(\psi_t(x))\big)\det\partial_x\psi_t(x)$ and $\operatorname{tr}\,\partial_xu_t=\operatorname{div}u_t$. Since the exponential is positive, the Jacobian matrix is invertible at every point, and the same argument applied to the backward ODE shows that $\psi_t^{-1}$ is continuously differentiable, so $\psi_t$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^d$. More generally, if the velocity field is of class $C^r$, then the flow is a $C^r$ diffeomorphism [@lipman2024guide, Theorem 1].

These statements require solutions for every starting point on all of $[0,1]$, and the velocity fields of flow matching do not always satisfy this. They can grow like $1/(1-t)$ as $t\to1$ (@eq-ot-vel), so linear growth with constants independent of $t$ can fail near $t=1$. An integrability condition on $u_t$ then takes the place of linear growth, but it gives a flow up to $t=1$ only for almost every starting point [@lipman2024guide, Section 3.4.1], and existence for almost every starting point does not make $\psi_t$ a bijection of $\mathbb{R}^d$. The results above are therefore not claimed for such fields on all of $\mathbb{R}^d$ at $t=1$. The conditional flow @eq-ot-flow is an example, because $\psi_t(\cdot\vert x_1)$ is a diffeomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^d$ for every $t<1$, whereas $\psi_1(x_0\vert x_1)=x_1$ for every $x_0$, so $\psi_1$ is not a bijection. More generally, if the distribution $q$ has no density, as for an empirical distribution, then $\psi_1$ cannot be a diffeomorphism, because a diffeomorphism maps a distribution with a density to a distribution with a density.

The results above describe a single trajectory, whereas generation starts from a random noise sample. Applying a flow to a random starting point $X_0\sim p_0$ gives a random point, and its distribution is called the push-forward of $p_0$. The push-forward is defined for any measurable map, so it needs the flow only at $p_0$-almost every starting point, which is what the integrability condition above provides for flow matching. If the flow is also a diffeomorphism, the push-forward has two further features. Since $\psi_t$ is a bijection, every point $x$ has exactly one preimage $\psi_t^{-1}(x)$, so the starting point of a sample can be recovered. Since $\psi_t$ and $\psi_t^{-1}$ are differentiable, the push-forward of a distribution with a density again has a density, which is given explicitly below. The push-forward can therefore be described by a family of densities, and if $X_0\sim p_0$ we set

$$
X_t:=\psi_t(X_0)\sim p_t .
$$ {#eq-flow-pushforward}

The density of $X_t$ is given by the change-of-variables formula, which applies because $\psi_t$ is a diffeomorphism. Explicitly, $p_t(x)=p_0\big(\psi_t^{-1}(x)\big)\,\big|\det\partial_x\psi_t^{-1}(x)\big|$.

@fig-grid shows the push-forward @eq-flow-pushforward at three times. The lines are the images of a square grid under $\psi_t$, and the points are samples of $X_t$. Since $\psi_t$ is a diffeomorphism, the grid is deformed continuously and the images of different grid lines do not cross, and the points move together with the grid. Where the grid cells are compressed the points are denser, and where they are stretched the points are sparser, which is the factor $\lvert\det\partial_x\psi_t^{-1}(x)\rvert$ in the density formula above.

![A flow $\psi_t$ at three times, increasing from left to right. The lines are the images of a square grid under $\psi_t$, and the black points are samples of $X_t=\psi_t(X_0)$, which start as samples of the source $X_0$ and move towards a target distribution. Figure 5 of @lipman2024guide, cropped from the lecture slides [@lecture-slides-flow].](figures/lec13/yws0322-slide07-flow-grid.png){#fig-grid width=100%}

Invertibility of the flow also allows it to be restarted at any time. Since $X_0=\psi_t^{-1}(X_t)$,

$$
X_s=\psi_s(X_0)=\psi_s\big(\psi_t^{-1}(X_t)\big)=:\psi_{s\vert t}(X_t),
$$ {#eq-restart}

and $\psi_{s\vert t}=\psi_s\circ\psi_t^{-1}$ is the solution of the same ODE started at time $t$. Indeed, differentiating in $s$ gives $\partial_s\psi_{s\vert t}(x)=u_s(\psi_{s\vert t}(x))$, and at $s=t$ the initial value is $\psi_t(\psi_t^{-1}(x))=x$.

With the flow and its push-forward in place, generation can be stated as a requirement on a flow. If a flow is chosen so that the push-forward of the noise distribution $p_0=p$ at $t=1$ is the data distribution $p_1=q$, then $\psi_1$ maps every noise sample to a sample of the data. Flow matching constructs such a flow in the four stages of @fig-blueprint, which the rest of Part I develops in turn. It starts from data, namely a source sample $X_0\sim p$ and a target sample $X_1\sim q$ (a). Path design then chooses the intermediate distributions, a probability path $p_t$ that interpolates between $p_0=p$ and $p_1=q$ (b). Training regresses a network $u_t^\theta$ on a velocity field $u_t$ that is known to generate this path, and this velocity field determines the flow through @eq-flow-ode (c). Finally, sampling integrates $u^\theta_t$ from $t=0$ to $t=1$, starting at a fresh noise sample (d).

![The four stages of flow matching. Panel (a) shows the data, a source sample $X_0\sim p$ (noise) and a target sample $X_1\sim q$ (an image). Panel (b) shows a probability path $p_t$ designed to interpolate between $p$ and $q$. Panel (c) shows training, in which the network $u_t^\theta(x)$ is regressed on a velocity field $u_t(x)$ that generates $p_t$. Panel (d) shows sampling, in which $u_t^\theta$ is integrated from a new noise sample at $t=0$ to a new data sample $X_1$ at $t=1$. Figure 2 of @lipman2024guide, cropped from the lecture slides [@lecture-slides-flow].](figures/lec13/yws0322-slide06-blueprint.png){#fig-blueprint width=100%}

### The velocity of a flow, and the Euler step {#sec-euler}

The flow was obtained from a velocity field by solving the ODE. Conversely, the velocity can be expressed in terms of the flow. Take a point $x$ at time $t$ and write $x'=\psi_t^{-1}(x)$ for the point it started from. Then @eq-flow-ode evaluated at $x'$ reads $\dot\psi_t(x')=u_t(\psi_t(x'))=u_t(x)$, that is

$$
u_t(x)=\dot\psi_t\big(\psi_t^{-1}(x)\big).
$$ {#eq-velocity-of-flow}

So $u_t$ is the velocity, at time $t$, of whichever trajectory passes through $x$, and this is the quantity that a network $u_t^\theta(x)$ has to reproduce.

Once a velocity field is available, sampling means integrating @eq-flow-ode numerically, and the simplest scheme for this is the Euler method. Since $t\mapsto\psi_t(x)$ is differentiable, Taylor's theorem gives

$$
X_{t+h}=X_t+h\,\dot X_t+o(h)=X_t+h\,u_t(X_t)+o(h),
$$ {#eq-euler}

and the scheme drops the remainder, giving $X_{t+h}\approx X_t+h\,u_t(X_t)$. One step is therefore exact to first order. Its error is $o(h)$ (and $O(h^2)$ when $u$ is $C^1$ in $(t,x)$), and these errors accumulate over the $1/h$ steps.

**A closed-form example.** Measuring this accumulated error requires a flow whose exact solution is known. Let $J(\xi_1,\xi_2)=(-\xi_2,\xi_1)$ be the rotation by $90^\circ$ and $\omega(r)=3e^{-r^2/2.2}$, and consider the velocity field $u(x)=\omega(\lVert x\rVert)\,Jx$. The radius is conserved along a trajectory, because $\tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\lVert\psi_t\rVert^2=2\,\psi_t\cdot u(\psi_t)=2\omega\,\psi_t\cdot J\psi_t=0$. Hence $\omega(\lVert\psi_t(x)\rVert)=\omega(\lVert x\rVert)$ is constant along the path and the ODE is a rotation at constant angular speed, with solution

$$
\psi_t(x)=R\big(t\,\omega(\lVert x\rVert)\big)\,x,
$$ {#eq-rotation}

with $R(\beta)$ the rotation by angle $\beta$. Since $\omega$ decreases with the radius, points near the origin rotate fastest. The grid is sheared where the angular speed changes with the radius, most strongly near $r=\sqrt{1.1}\approx1.05$, where $\lvert\omega'(r)\rvert$ is largest, and it turns almost rigidly near the origin, where $\omega'(0)=0$ (panels 1 to 3 of @fig-flow). The samples of $X_0$ move together with the grid, so the round cloud at $t=0$ becomes a curved band, and the distribution of this band is the push-forward @eq-flow-pushforward of the Gaussian by this flow. Now run Euler from $x_0=(1,0)$ with $h=0.25$. Because $Jx\perp x$ and $\lVert Jx\rVert=\lVert x\rVert$, one Euler step multiplies the radius by $\sqrt{1+h^2\omega(r)^2}>1$, whereas the exact flow keeps it at $1$. The radius therefore grows at every step (@tbl-euler).

| step $k$ | $r_k$ | $\omega(r_k)$ | $h\,\omega(r_k)$ | $r_{k+1}=r_k\sqrt{1+(h\omega)^2}$ |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| 0 | 1.000 | 1.904 | 0.476 | 1.108 |
| 1 | 1.108 | 1.718 | 0.429 | 1.205 |
| 2 | 1.205 | 1.550 | 0.387 | 1.293 |
| 3 | 1.293 | 1.404 | 0.351 | 1.370 |

: Four Euler steps of size $h=0.25$ on the rotation field, started at radius $1$. The exact flow stays at radius $1$. {#tbl-euler}

The last panel of @fig-flow shows the resulting path, along which the radius increases. The error arises because the velocity changes direction along the exact trajectory, whereas an Euler step keeps the velocity fixed over the whole interval. In general the Euler method is accurate when the velocity changes little along the path. If $u_t(x_t)$ is constant along a trajectory, that is, if the trajectory is a straight line traversed at constant speed, then one Euler step is exact. A straight line traversed at varying speed does not have this property, because for $x_t=t^2$ the velocity $2t$ changes and one step has error $h^2$. Trajectories that are close to straight lines at constant speed can therefore be followed with few steps, which is why such paths are relevant for sampling.

![A flow as a push-forward, and the Euler step. Panels 1 to 3 show the flow of @eq-rotation applied to a grid ($\psi_t$) and to samples of a Gaussian $X_0$ ($X_t=\psi_t(X_0)$) at $t=0,\,0.5,\,1$. Panel 4 shows the velocity field $u$ (arrow shade = speed), the exact trajectory from $x_0=(1,0)$ (radius $1$) and four Euler steps of size $h=0.25$, along which the radius increases to $1.37$ (@tbl-euler).](figures/lec13/yws0322-f1-flow-pushforward.png){#fig-flow width=100%}

## Probability paths and the continuity equation {#sec-ce}

@sec-flow-fields defined the flow of a velocity field and the push-forward of a distribution under it. Generation is a statement about the distributions $p_t$, so this section characterises the velocity fields that produce a given family of distributions. The push-forward @eq-flow-pushforward assigns a family of densities to each velocity field and starting density. In general, a probability path is a family of densities $p_t$, $t\in[0,1]$, that is continuous in $t$, and a velocity field $u_t$ generates $p_t$ if the flow of $u_t$, applied to a sample of $p_0$, gives a sample of $p_t$ at every time

$$
X_t=\psi_t(X_0)\sim p_t\quad\text{for all }t\in[0,1],\ \text{when }X_0\sim p_0 .
$$ {#eq-generates}

Checking this definition directly requires solving the ODE, which is impractical for every candidate field. The continuity equation replaces it by a local condition, which involves only derivatives of $p_t$ and $u_t$ at each point. We say that $p_t$ and $u_t$ satisfy the continuity equation if

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}p_t(x)+\operatorname{div}(p_tu_t)(x)=0,\qquad t\in[0,1].
$$ {#eq-ce}

::: {#thm-ce}
## Mass conservation
Let $u_t$ be a velocity field that is continuous in $(t,x)$, whose derivative $\partial_xu_t(x)$ is continuous in $(t,x)$, and whose solutions exist on $[0,1]$ in both directions (for example under linear growth), so that its flow is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism by @sec-flow-def. Let $p_t$ be a probability path that is $C^1$ in $(t,x)$. Then the continuity equation @eq-ce holds for all $t\in[0,1]$ if and only if $u_t$ generates $p_t$ in the sense of @eq-generates.
:::

@eq-ce is understood pointwise, which is why $p_t$ and $u_t$ are assumed to be differentiable. The direction from generation to the continuity equation is a computation with a test function, and the converse direction follows the trajectories of the flow and uses the Jacobian formula @eq-jacobian.

::: {.proof}
We first show that generation implies the continuity equation. Let $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)$ have support $K$, and let $M=\sup_{t\in[0,1],\,x\in K}\lVert u_t(x)\rVert$, which is finite because $u$ is continuous. If $X_0\sim p_0$ and $X_t=\psi_t(X_0)\sim p_t$, then $\mathbb{E}\,\varphi(X_t)=\int\varphi\,p_t\,\mathrm{d}x$. By the chain rule and @eq-flow-ode, $\tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\varphi(\psi_t(x_0))=\nabla\varphi(\psi_t(x_0))\cdot u_t(\psi_t(x_0))$, and this is at most $M\sup_x\lVert\nabla\varphi(x)\rVert$ in absolute value for every $x_0$ and $t$, because it vanishes unless $\psi_t(x_0)\in K$. The bound does not depend on $x_0$ and $t$, so differentiation under the expectation is allowed by dominated convergence. In the same way $\tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int\varphi\,p_t\,\mathrm{d}x=\int\varphi\,\partial_tp_t\,\mathrm{d}x$, because $\partial_tp_t$ is continuous and $\varphi$ has compact support. Hence

$$
\int\varphi\,\partial_tp_t\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}\,\varphi(X_t)=\mathbb{E}\big[\nabla\varphi(X_t)\cdot u_t(X_t)\big]=\int\nabla\varphi\cdot u_t\,p_t\,\mathrm{d}x=-\int\varphi\,\operatorname{div}(p_tu_t)\,\mathrm{d}x,
$$

where the last step is integration by parts ($p_tu_t$ is $C^1$ in $x$ and $\varphi$ has compact support, so there is no boundary term). Hence $\int\varphi\,\big(\partial_tp_t+\operatorname{div}(p_tu_t)\big)\mathrm{d}x=0$ for every test function $\varphi$, and since the bracket is continuous in $x$, it vanishes at every point, which is @eq-ce.

We now show that the continuity equation implies generation. Fix $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and put $g(t)=p_t(\psi_t(x))\,\det\partial_x\psi_t(x)$. By the chain rule and @eq-flow-ode, $\tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}p_t(\psi_t(x))=\big(\partial_tp_t+\nabla p_t\cdot u_t\big)(\psi_t(x))$, and by @eq-jacobian, $\tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\det\partial_x\psi_t(x)=\operatorname{div}u_t(\psi_t(x))\,\det\partial_x\psi_t(x)$. Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}
g'(t)&=\big(\partial_tp_t+\nabla p_t\cdot u_t+p_t\operatorname{div}u_t\big)(\psi_t(x))\,\det\partial_x\psi_t(x)\\
&=\big(\partial_tp_t+\operatorname{div}(p_tu_t)\big)(\psi_t(x))\,\det\partial_x\psi_t(x)=0
\end{aligned}
$$

by @eq-ce. So $g(t)=g(0)=p_0(x)$, that is, $p_t(\psi_t(x))\,\det\partial_x\psi_t(x)=p_0(x)$. Now let $X_0\sim p_0$ and let $f$ be a bounded measurable function. Since $\psi_t$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism with positive Jacobian determinant, the change of variables $y=\psi_t(x)$ gives

$$
\mathbb{E}\,f(\psi_t(X_0))=\int f(\psi_t(x))\,p_0(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\int f(\psi_t(x))\,p_t(\psi_t(x))\,\det\partial_x\psi_t(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\int f(y)\,p_t(y)\,\mathrm{d}y,
$$

so $\psi_t(X_0)\sim p_t$, which says that $u_t$ generates $p_t$.
:::

The theorem is stated for $C^1$ fields so that every term of @eq-ce exists pointwise. For fields that are only locally Lipschitz in $x$ and integrable in $t$, the continuity equation is read in the weak sense, and the weak form has to contain the initial distribution,

$$
\int_0^1\!\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}p_t\,(\partial_t\varphi+u_t\cdot\nabla\varphi)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t+\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\varphi(0,x)\,p_0(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=0\quad\text{for all }\varphi\in C_c^\infty\big([0,1)\times\mathbb{R}^d\big),
$$ {#eq-ce-weak}

because test functions supported in $(0,1)\times\mathbb{R}^d$ do not involve $p_0$. For such test functions every constant path $p_t=\bar p$ satisfies the equation when $u=0$, whereas the flow of $u=0$ generates only the constant path equal to $p_0$. The existence of the flow for every starting point is replaced by the integrability condition $\int_0^1\!\int\lVert u_t(x)\rVert\,p_t(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t<\infty$ [@lipman2024guide, Section 3.5], which gives a flow for $p_0$-almost every starting point, and this is all that @eq-generates needs [@lipman2024guide, Section 3.4.1]. Theorem 2 of @lipman2024guide states, for $t\in[0,1)$, the equivalence of generation and the continuity equation, which in this generality is read as @eq-ce-weak, provided that $u$ is measurable and locally Lipschitz in $x$ and that $p_t$ is continuous in $t$. This theorem is stated on $[0,1)$ because the velocity fields of flow matching can be singular at $t=1$, so it gives @eq-generates only for $t<1$. Generation at $t=1$ follows if in addition the flow extends to $t=1$ for $p_0$-almost every starting point and $p_t\to p_1$ weakly as $t\to1$, because then $\mathbb{E}f(X_t)\to\mathbb{E}f(X_1)$ and $\int f\,p_t\,\mathrm{d}x\to\int f\,p_1\,\mathrm{d}x$ for every bounded continuous $f$. The proof above covers the case in which every term exists pointwise, and the general case is quoted.

The theorem is called mass conservation because @eq-ce keeps $\int p_t\,\mathrm{d}x$ constant for every family of nonnegative, integrable $C^1$ functions $p_t$ that solves it with a velocity field satisfying the hypotheses of @thm-ce, whether or not it is a probability path, provided that the integrability condition above holds. To see this, let $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)$ satisfy $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on the unit ball, and put $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$. Since $\chi_R$ has compact support and $\partial_tp_t$ is continuous, differentiation under the integral is allowed, and @eq-ce with integration by parts gives the first line below. Since $\lVert\nabla\chi_R\rVert\le c/R$ with $c=\sup\lVert\nabla\chi\rVert$, integration over $[s,t]$ gives the second line,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int\chi_R\,p_t\,\mathrm{d}x&=-\int\chi_R\operatorname{div}(p_tu_t)\,\mathrm{d}x=\int\nabla\chi_R\cdot u_t\,p_t\,\mathrm{d}x,\\
\Big\lvert\int\chi_R\,p_t\,\mathrm{d}x-\int\chi_R\,p_s\,\mathrm{d}x\Big\rvert&\le\frac{c}{R}\int_0^1\!\int\lVert u_\tau(x)\rVert\,p_\tau(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}\tau .
\end{aligned}
$$

As $R\to\infty$ the right-hand side tends to zero, and the left-hand side tends to $\lvert\int p_t\,\mathrm{d}x-\int p_s\,\mathrm{d}x\rvert$ by dominated convergence, because $\lvert\chi_Rp_t\rvert\le p_t$. Hence the total mass is the same at all times, so if $p_0$ integrates to $1$ then every $p_t$ does, which says that probability is neither created nor destroyed. Accordingly, $p_tu_t$ is called the flux of probability mass. Without the integrability condition mass can leave through infinity, as for $u(x)=x^2$.

**Example (a Gaussian with time-dependent variance).** Let $p_t=\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_t^2I)$ with $\sigma_t>0$ continuously differentiable on $[0,1]$. Its flow is $\psi_t(x)=(\sigma_t/\sigma_0)x$, so the velocity is $u_t(x)=\dot\psi_t(\psi_t^{-1}(x))=(\dot\sigma_t/\sigma_t)\,x$ by @eq-velocity-of-flow. We now check directly that this pair satisfies @eq-ce. From $\log p_t(x)=-\tfrac d2\log(2\pi\sigma_t^2)-\lVert x\rVert^2/(2\sigma_t^2)$,

$$
\partial_t\log p_t=-\frac{d\,\dot\sigma_t}{\sigma_t}+\frac{\lVert x\rVert^2\dot\sigma_t}{\sigma_t^3},\qquad
\frac{\operatorname{div}(p_tu_t)}{p_t}=\operatorname{div}u_t+u_t\cdot\nabla\log p_t=\frac{d\,\dot\sigma_t}{\sigma_t}-\frac{\lVert x\rVert^2\dot\sigma_t}{\sigma_t^3},
$$

and the two terms sum to zero, as @thm-ce requires. This example is used again in @sec-gauss.

## Flow matching {#sec-fm}

### Problem definition {#sec-fm-problem}

@sec-ce shows how to check whether a velocity field generates a given path, but it does not provide a velocity field. Flow matching therefore poses the following task, which is to find a velocity field $u_t^\theta$ that generates a probability path $p_t$ with $p_0=p$ and $p_1=q$. If we had such a path and knew a velocity field $u_t$ that generates it, we could train a network by regression,

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{X_t\sim p_t}\,D\big(u_t(X_t),\,u_t^\theta(X_t)\big),
$$ {#eq-lfm-generic}

where $D$ is a dissimilarity (in practice the squared Euclidean distance) and the expectation also averages over $t$. After training, sampling is numerical integration of the learned ODE, as in @sec-euler. Constructing a suitable path requires three objects.

- A coupling $(X_0,X_1)\sim\pi_{0,1}(X_0,X_1)$ of source and target samples. The simplest choice is independence, $\pi_{0,1}=p\otimes q$, which needs no pairing of the data.
- A conditional path $p_{t\vert1}(\cdot\vert x_1)$ for each target point $x_1$ that starts at the source, $p_{0\vert1}(\cdot\vert x_1)=p$, and ends at the point, $p_{1\vert1}(\cdot\vert x_1)=\delta_{x_1}$. The start $p$ assumes the independent coupling, and for a general coupling the conditional path starts at the conditional law of $X_0$ given $X_1=x_1$.
- The marginal path obtained by averaging the conditional ones over the data,

$$
p_t(x)=\int p_{t\vert1}(x\vert x_1)\,q(x_1)\,\mathrm{d}x_1 .
$$ {#eq-marginal-path}

The boundary conditions of the conditional paths make this a path from $p$ to $q$. At $t=0$ the integrand is $p(x)q(x_1)$, so $p_0=p$, and at $t=1$ it is $\delta_{x_1}(x)q(x_1)$, so $p_1=q$. @fig-path-design shows a conditional path, which starts at $p$ and concentrates at $x_1$ (a), and the marginal path, which moves from $p$ to $q$ (b). Sampling from $p_t$ is also easy, because one can draw $X_1\sim q$ and then $X_t\sim p_{t\vert1}(\cdot\vert X_1)$. This $X_t$ has the law $p_t$, but in general it is not the point $\psi_t(X_0)$ of the marginal flow, and from here on $X_t$ denotes a sample drawn in this way. The difficulty lies in the regression target. The field $u_t$ in @eq-lfm-generic is the velocity of the marginal path, and it is not known. Each conditional path, in contrast, has a conditional velocity $u_t(x\vert x_1)$ that can be written explicitly, and for the straight-line paths used later it points from $x$ towards $x_1$ (@fig-path-design, c). The marginal velocity at $x$ is a weighted average of the conditional velocities towards all target points (d), and the next section derives this average and its weights.

![Conditional and marginal objects of flow matching for a Gaussian source $p$ and a target $q$. Panel (a) shows a conditional probability path $p_t(\cdot\vert x_1)$, which starts at $p$ and concentrates at the target point $x_1$. Panel (b) shows the marginal probability path $p_t$ from $p$ to $q$. Panel (c) shows the conditional velocity field $u_t(\cdot\vert x_1)$, which generates the path of panel (a). Panel (d) shows the marginal velocity $u_t(x)$ (red), which is obtained by averaging the conditional velocities towards different target points such as $x_1$ and $x_1'$ (black). Figure 3 of @lipman2024guide, cropped from the lecture slides [@lecture-slides-flow].](figures/lec13/yws0322-slide10-path-design.png){#fig-path-design width=100% fig-pos="H"}

### Conditioning {#sec-conditioning}

So far the conditional paths were indexed by the target point $x_1$, but the same construction works with any conditioning variable. One can condition on the target $X_1$, on the source $X_0$, or on the pair $(X_0,X_1)$, and in each case the path and the velocity are averages of conditional ones (@tbl-conditioning). @fig-conditioning shows the conditional paths of the three cases, with the source distribution on the left and the target distribution on the right of each panel. Conditioning on $X_1$ fixes one target point $x_1$, and the conditional path then leads from the whole source distribution to that point (left). Conditioning on $X_0$ fixes one source point, and the conditional path leads from that point to the whole target distribution (middle). Conditioning on the pair fixes both points, and the conditional path is a single path from $x_0$ to $x_1$ (right). The more variables are fixed, the simpler the conditional path is, and in each case averaging over the fixed variables gives a marginal path from $p$ to $q$ (@tbl-conditioning).

| conditioning on | marginal path $p_t(x)$ | marginal velocity $u_t(x)$ |
|:-----|:-------------|:---------|
| $X_1$ | $\int p_{t\vert1}(x\vert x_1)\,q(x_1)\,\mathrm{d}x_1$ | $\mathbb{E}\big[u_t(X_t\vert X_1)\,\big\vert\,X_t=x\big]$ |
| $X_0$ | $\int p_{t\vert0}(x\vert x_0)\,p(x_0)\,\mathrm{d}x_0$ | $\mathbb{E}\big[u_t(X_t\vert X_0)\,\big\vert\,X_t=x\big]$ |
| $(X_0,X_1)$ | $\int p_{t\vert0,1}(x\vert x_0,x_1)\,\pi_{0,1}(x_0,x_1)\,\mathrm{d}x_0\mathrm{d}x_1$ | $\mathbb{E}\big[u_t(X_t\vert X_0,X_1)\,\big\vert\,X_t=x\big]$ |

: The three conditionings. {#tbl-conditioning}

![The three conditionings of @tbl-conditioning, for a source density (left in each panel) and a target density (right). Conditioning on $X_1$ gives conditional paths from the whole source to one target point $x_1$. Conditioning on $X_0$ gives paths from one source point $x_0$ to the whole target. Conditioning on the pair gives a single path from $x_0$ to $x_1$. The bottom row gives the conditional flow and the conditional path of each case. The upper part of Figure 11 of @lipman2024guide, cropped from the lecture slides [@lecture-slides-flow].](figures/lec13/yws0322-slide11-conditioning.png){#fig-conditioning width=100%}

All three cases have the same structure, so they can be treated together. Let $Z\sim\pi$ be the conditioning variable ($X_1$, $X_0$ or $(X_0,X_1)$), with conditional path $p_t(\cdot\vert z)$ and conditional velocity $u_t(\cdot\vert z)$. Define

$$
p_t(x)=\int p_t(x\vert z)\,\pi(z)\,\mathrm{d}z,\qquad
u_t(x)=\int u_t(x\vert z)\,\frac{p_t(x\vert z)\,\pi(z)}{p_t(x)}\,\mathrm{d}z=\mathbb{E}\big[u_t(X_t\vert Z)\,\big\vert\,X_t=x\big].
$$ {#eq-marginal-vel}

The velocity $u_t(x)$ is defined at every $x$ with $p_t(x)>0$, and its second form follows from Bayes' rule. Given $X_t=x$, the conditioning variable has the posterior density $p_t(x\vert z)\pi(z)/p_t(x)$, so the marginal velocity is the conditional velocity averaged over the posterior of $Z$. The following theorem shows that this average is the correct regression target, because it generates the marginal path.

::: {#thm-marg}
## Marginalization theorem
Assume $p_t(x)>0$ for all $x$ and all $t\in[0,1)$, and the regularity that allows differentiation and integration to be exchanged. If for every $z$ the conditional velocity $u_t(\cdot\vert z)$ generates the conditional path $p_t(\cdot\vert z)$ for $t\in[0,1)$, then the marginal velocity $u_t$ generates the marginal path $p_t$ for $t\in[0,1)$ (both are defined in @eq-marginal-vel).
:::

::: {.proof}
By @thm-ce, applied on $[0,T]$ for every $T<1$, each pair $(p_t(\cdot\vert z),u_t(\cdot\vert z))$ satisfies the continuity equation for $t<1$. Differentiate the marginal path in $t$, exchange derivative and integral, apply the conditional continuity equation, and exchange the divergence and the integral

$$
\begin{aligned}
\partial_tp_t(x)&=\int\partial_tp_t(x\vert z)\,\pi(z)\,\mathrm{d}z
=-\int\operatorname{div}_x\big(p_t(x\vert z)\,u_t(x\vert z)\big)\,\pi(z)\,\mathrm{d}z\\
&=-\operatorname{div}_x\Big(\int u_t(x\vert z)\,p_t(x\vert z)\,\pi(z)\,\mathrm{d}z\Big)
=-\operatorname{div}_x\big(p_t(x)\,u_t(x)\big),
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-marg-proof}

where the last equality is the definition of $u_t$ in @eq-marginal-vel (multiply it by $p_t(x)$). So $(p_t,u_t)$ satisfies the continuity equation for $t<1$, and @thm-ce, again on $[0,T]$ for every $T<1$, says that $u_t$ generates $p_t$ for $t<1$ (the hypotheses of @thm-ce on $u_t$ are part of the regularity assumed).
:::

The proof differentiates the conditional densities pointwise, which is not possible when the conditional path is a point mass, as for $Z=(X_0,X_1)$ below. In that case the conditional continuity equation holds in the weak (test-function) sense of the proof of @thm-ce, and the same computation goes through with a test function in place of pointwise values. The theorem is stated for $t<1$ because a conditional path that ends at a point mass, such as the Gaussian path of @sec-ot, has no density at $t=1$ and its conditional velocity is singular there. Generation at $t=1$ then follows under the two additional conditions given in @sec-ce, namely that the flow extends to $t=1$ and that $p_t$ converges weakly to $q$.

**A worked example with numbers.** The posterior average in @eq-marginal-vel can be computed by hand in a small case. Take $d=2$, source $p=\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ and a target of two equally likely points $A=(2,1)$ and $B=(2,-1)$. Condition on $X_1$ and use the Gaussian path of @sec-ot, $p_{t\vert1}(x\vert x_1)=\mathcal{N}(x\,\vert\,tx_1,(1-t)^2I)$ with $u_t(x\vert x_1)=(x_1-x)/(1-t)$. At $t=\tfrac12$ and the point $x^*=(1.0,\,0.3)$ the conditional velocities are

$$
u_A=\frac{A-x^*}{1-t}=(2.0,\,1.4),\qquad u_B=\frac{B-x^*}{1-t}=(2.0,\,-2.6).
$$

The posterior weight of each target is proportional to $p_{t\vert1}(x^*\vert x_1)\cdot\tfrac12$. Here $tA=(1.0,0.5)$ and $tB=(1.0,-0.5)$, so $\lVert x^*-tA\rVert^2=0.04$ and $\lVert x^*-tB\rVert^2=0.64$, and with $2(1-t)^2=0.5$,

$$
w_A=\frac{e^{-0.04/0.5}}{e^{-0.04/0.5}+e^{-0.64/0.5}}=\frac{1}{1+e^{-1.2}}=0.7685,\qquad w_B=0.2315 .
$$

The marginal velocity is the weighted average,

$$
u_t(x^*)=w_Au_A+w_Bu_B=(2.0,\ 0.7685\cdot1.4-0.2315\cdot2.6)=(2.00,\ 0.474).
$$

@fig-marginal shows the three fields, and it is a computed version of panel (d) of @fig-path-design. As the weights predict, the marginal arrow lies between the two conditional ones and closer to $u_A$, the velocity towards the target that is more probable at $x^*$. The formula can also be checked by simulation. A Monte Carlo estimate (average of $X_1-X_0$ over $6\times10^6$ simulated pairs with $X_t$ within $0.06$ of $x^*$) gave $(2.001,\,0.494)$, with standard errors of about $0.0004$ and $0.010$. The second component is about two standard errors from $0.474$, which is within the usual range of Monte Carlo variation.

![Conditional and marginal velocity at $t=0.5$ for $p=\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ and a target of two points $A=(2,1)$ and $B=(2,-1)$. Panels (a) and (b) show the conditional fields $u_t(x\vert x_1)=(x_1-x)/(1-t)$ for $x_1=A$ and $x_1=B$, and the contours show the marginal density $p_t$. Panel (c) shows the marginal field, which is the posterior-weighted average of the two. At $x^*=(1.0,0.3)$ the weights are $w_A=0.77$ and $w_B=0.23$ and $u_t(x^*)=(2.00,0.47)$ (black). The three arrows at $x^*$ are drawn 2.2 times longer than the field arrows.](figures/lec13/yws0322-f3-cond-vs-marginal.png){#fig-marginal width=100%}

**Straight conditional paths and curved marginal trajectories.** In the example above the conditional path $\mathcal{N}(tx_1,(1-t)^2I)$ is the law of $tx_1+(1-t)X_0$, so a sample moves along a straight line from $X_0$ towards $x_1$, and the same holds for a fixed pair $(X_0,X_1)$. The trajectories of the marginal velocity, however, are in general not straight. A one-dimensional example shows the difference. Take $X_0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and a data distribution that is a mixture of two narrow Gaussians centred at $\pm1.5$, and draw independent pairs. The lines $x_t=(1-t)x_0+tx_1$ then cross in the $(t,x)$ plane (@fig-lines, left). The integral curves of the marginal velocity, in contrast, cannot cross, because a locally Lipschitz field has exactly one trajectory through each point, and in this example they are curved (middle). Although the two families of curves differ, they have the same distribution $p_t$ at every time, and in particular the endpoints of the integral curves have the distribution $q$ (right). The same example shows what the network learns from the pairs. In training, each noise sample $x_0$ is paired with a data sample $x_1$ at random (the independent coupling), but the network receives only $(x_t,t)$ and never the pairing. It therefore learns the marginal velocity $u_t(x)=\mathbb{E}[X_1-X_0\vert X_t=x]$, the average over all pairs whose interpolation passes through $x$ at time $t$. The flow of this field maps each noise sample to some data point, in general not the one it was paired with, while the endpoints as a whole still have the distribution $q$. The pairing thus appears only in the loss, through the sampling of $(X_0,X_1)$.

![The left panel shows straight conditional paths of independent pairs, which cross ($X_0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and $X_1$ a mixture of two narrow Gaussians at $\pm1.5$). The middle panel shows integral curves of the exact marginal velocity from the same starting points, which never cross. The right panel shows that endpoints of the marginal ODE started from $2\times10^4$ noise samples match the data density $q$ (Wasserstein-1 distance $0.014$ in one draw, while two independent data samples are $0.011$ apart, so the two agree within sampling variation). The exact marginal velocity for this example is derived in @sec-beyond.](figures/lec13/yws0322-f4-lines-vs-ode.png){#fig-lines width=100%}

### The losses, and why they have the same gradient {#sec-loss}

With the marginal velocity in hand, we define the two losses. For $t\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1]$ and the squared Euclidean distance,

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t,\,X_t\sim p_t}\big\lVert u_t^\theta(X_t)-u_t(X_t)\big\rVert^2,\qquad
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t,\,Z\sim\pi,\,X_t\sim p_t(\cdot\vert Z)}\big\lVert u_t^\theta(X_t)-u_t(X_t\vert Z)\big\rVert^2 .
$$ {#eq-losses}

The first loss needs the marginal velocity $u_t$, which is not available, whereas the second needs only the conditional velocity, which is known in closed form. The following theorem shows that training on the second loss is nevertheless equivalent to training on the first.

::: {#thm-cfm}
## Gradient equivalence of FM and CFM
Assume $\mathbb{E}\lVert u_t(X_t\vert Z)\rVert^2<\infty$ and $\mathbb{E}\lVert u_t^\theta(X_t)\rVert^2<\infty$. Then $\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta)=\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta)$ wherever either side exists. More precisely,

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta)+C,\qquad C=\mathbb{E}\big\lVert u_t(X_t\vert Z)-u_t(X_t)\big\rVert^2\ \ge 0,
$$ {#eq-cfm-gap}

where $C$ does not depend on $\theta$. In particular, if $u_t^\theta$ ranges over all velocity fields, the minimiser of $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}$ is the marginal velocity $u_t$. For a restricted family such as a neural network, the two losses have the same minimisers in the family, namely the members closest to $u_t$ in $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}$, and these equal $u_t$ only if $u_t$ belongs to the family.
:::

The theorem holds for any Bregman divergence $D(a,b)$ with the target as first and the network output as second argument, as in @eq-lfm-generic [@lipman2024guide, Theorem 4]. The proof below treats the squared error, for which the arguments are interchangeable.

::: {.proof}
Expand both squares as $\lVert a-b\rVert^2=\lVert a\rVert^2-2\,a\cdot b+\lVert b\rVert^2$ and compare the three terms. For every $t$ draw $Z\sim\pi$ and then $X_t\sim p_t(\cdot\vert Z)$. By @eq-marginal-vel the law of $X_t$ is $p_t$, and by the integrability assumption every expectation below is finite (the cross terms by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality).

The quadratic term in $u^\theta$ is $\mathbb{E}_{Z,X_t}\lVert u^\theta_t(X_t)\rVert^2=\int\lVert u^\theta_t(x)\rVert^2p_t(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$, which is the same in both losses.

For the cross term, the tower property of conditional expectation and the second form of @eq-marginal-vel give
$$
\mathbb{E}_{Z,X_t}\big[u^\theta_t(X_t)\cdot u_t(X_t\vert Z)\big]
=\mathbb{E}\Big[u^\theta_t(X_t)\cdot\mathbb{E}\big[u_t(X_t\vert Z)\,\big\vert\,X_t\big]\Big]
=\mathbb{E}\big[u^\theta_t(X_t)\cdot u_t(X_t)\big],
$$
which is the cross term of $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}$. This form also covers a conditional path that is a point mass, as for $Z=(X_0,X_1)$, for which $p_t(\cdot\vert z)$ has no density.

The last terms $\mathbb{E}\lVert u_t(X_t\vert Z)\rVert^2$ and $\mathbb{E}\lVert u_t(X_t)\rVert^2$ do not involve $\theta$.

Hence $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}=\mathbb{E}\lVert u_t(X_t\vert Z)\rVert^2-\mathbb{E}\lVert u_t(X_t)\rVert^2$ is a constant, and the gradients agree. To identify the constant, apply the cross-term identity with $u^\theta$ replaced by $u_t$, which gives $\mathbb{E}[u_t(X_t)\cdot u_t(X_t\vert Z)]=\mathbb{E}\lVert u_t(X_t)\rVert^2$. Then
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\lVert u_t(X_t\vert Z)-u_t(X_t)\rVert^2&=\mathbb{E}\lVert u_t(X_t\vert Z)\rVert^2-2\,\mathbb{E}\lVert u_t(X_t)\rVert^2+\mathbb{E}\lVert u_t(X_t)\rVert^2\\
&=\mathbb{E}\lVert u_t(X_t\vert Z)\rVert^2-\mathbb{E}\lVert u_t(X_t)\rVert^2=C .
\end{aligned}
$$
Finally $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}\ge0$, with equality exactly when $u^\theta_t=u_t$ almost everywhere with respect to the distribution of $(t,X_t)$. Since $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}+C$, the two losses have the same minimisers, and if the family of fields $u^\theta_t$ contains $u_t$, then $u^\theta=u_t$ is the minimiser and the minimum value of $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}$ is $C$.
:::

The theorem has two practical consequences. First, $C$ is the minimum value of $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}$ if the network can represent $u_t$ and a lower bound otherwise, and it equals the mean squared deviation of the conditional velocity from its posterior mean $u_t(X_t)$. Since no network can reduce $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}$ below $C$, a loss curve that stays at a positive value is expected (as in @fig-practice). Second, the stochastic gradients of the two losses have the same mean, so stochastic gradient descent on the computable $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}$ has the same expected update direction as descent on the intractable $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}$.

**Checking the theorem numerically.** The theorem can be tested on the one-dimensional example of @fig-lines, because there $u_t$ is known exactly. Take the family $v_\theta=u_t+\theta g$ with $g(x,t)=\tanh(x)\,(\tfrac12+t)$ and the conditioning $Z=(X_0,X_1)$, whose conditional velocity is $X_1-X_0$, and put $a=u_t(X_t)-(X_1-X_0)$. Then $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta)=\theta^2\,\mathbb{E}[g^2]$ and $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}[a^2]+2\theta\,\mathbb{E}[ag]+\theta^2\mathbb{E}[g^2]$, so the theorem predicts $\mathbb{E}[ag]=0$ and $C=\mathbb{E}[a^2]$. With $3\times10^6$ samples, $\mathbb{E}[g^2]=0.609$, $C=\mathbb{E}[a^2]=2.043$ and $\mathbb{E}[ag]=+0.00036\pm0.00048$, which is zero within Monte Carlo error. Panel (a) of @fig-thm4 shows that the two losses differ by the constant $C$ at every $\theta$ up to Monte Carlo error, so they have the same minimiser, and panel (b) shows that their gradients coincide up to the same error.

![Numerical check of @thm-cfm. Panel (a) shows that the two losses along the family $v_\theta=u_t+\theta g$ differ by the constant $C=2.043$ at every $\theta$, up to Monte Carlo error. Panel (b) shows that their gradients coincide. The two gradients differ by the constant $2\,\mathbb{E}[a\,g]=+0.0007$, with standard error $0.0010$ ($N=3\times10^6$ samples), which is zero within Monte Carlo error.](figures/lec13/yws0322-f6-theorem4-check.png){#fig-thm4 width=100%}

### The objects of flow matching {#sec-map}

@fig-map reproduces the lecture's summary diagram of the objects introduced so far and of the operations between them. The relations fall into two groups.

Within one row, the flow, the velocity field and the probability path are related in the following way. A flow determines its velocity by differentiation (@eq-velocity-of-flow), and a velocity determines its flow by solving the ODE (@eq-flow-ode). The flow determines the path as the push-forward of $p_0$ (@eq-flow-pushforward). A velocity and a path that it generates satisfy the continuity equation (@thm-ce), whereas the reverse direction, from a path to a velocity, has no unique solution.
Between the rows, the conditional velocity and path of the middle row are explicit and the marginal velocity and path of the top row are not, so the marginal ones are obtained from the conditional ones by averaging. The marginal flow is not obtained by averaging. It follows from the marginal velocity by solving the ODE. The marginal path is the average of the conditional paths (@eq-marginal-path), and the marginal velocity is the average of the conditional velocities weighted by the posterior of the conditioning variable (@eq-marginal-vel). The marginalization theorem (@thm-marg) states that this averaged velocity generates the averaged path, and the boundary conditions $p_0=p$ and $p_1=q$ of the marginal path follow from the conditional ones, $p_{0\vert1}=p$ and $p_{1\vert1}=\delta_{x_1}$, because averaging over $x_1\sim q$ preserves them. The same passage from conditional to marginal relates the two losses. The FM loss regresses the network on the unknown marginal velocity, the CFM loss regresses it on the known conditional velocity, and the two have the same gradient (@thm-cfm), so training uses only the conditional row. The bottom row is the Gaussian instance used in practice, with the flow @eq-ot-flow, the velocity @eq-ot-vel and the path @eq-ot-path.

![The objects of flow matching and the operations between them. The top row contains the marginal flow, velocity field and probability path, the middle row the same objects conditional on $X_1$, and the bottom row the Gaussian/OT instance of @sec-ot. The horizontal arrows show that differentiating a flow gives its velocity, that solving the ODE recovers the flow, and that the continuity equation links a velocity to the path it generates, while the reverse direction from a path to a velocity has no unique solution. The vertical arrows show that the marginal velocity and path are the conditional expectation and the marginalisation of the conditional ones. The two right-hand columns give the boundary conditions and the loss of each row. Blue arrows mark the relations that flow matching uses. Figure 9 of @lipman2024guide, cropped from the lecture slides [@lecture-slides-flow], where the numbers in parentheses are equation numbers of that paper.](figures/lec13/yws0322-slide13-objects.png){#fig-map width=88%}

The non-uniqueness of the velocity has a simple reason, because many velocity fields generate the same path. If $u_t$ generates $p_t$ and $\tilde u_t$ satisfies $\operatorname{div}(p_t\tilde u_t)=0$, then $u_t+\tilde u_t$ satisfies the same continuity equation (the equation is linear in $u_t$), so it generates $p_t$ too. For $p_t=\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ in the plane the rotation field $\tilde u(x)=Jx$ is such a field, because $\operatorname{div}Jx=0$ and $x\perp Jx$ give $\operatorname{div}(p\,Jx)=p\,(\operatorname{div}Jx-x\cdot Jx)=0$. For this reason flow matching does not look for the velocity field of a given path. It chooses the path first and then constructs one particular velocity field for it, the marginal velocity of @eq-marginal-vel.

## Gaussian and affine conditional paths {#sec-gauss}

The previous section concluded that flow matching chooses the path first. The marginalization theorem holds for any conditional paths, so the choice of the conditional path is still open, and from here on the conditional paths are Gaussian, because for them every object has a closed form.

### Gaussian conditional flow matching {#sec-ot}

Let the source be $p=\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ and condition on $X_1=x_1$. Take the conditional flow that maps the noise sample $x_0$ linearly to $x_1$,

$$
\psi_t(x_0\vert x_1)=t\,x_1+(1-t)\,x_0 .
$$ {#eq-ot-flow}

Applying it to $X_0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ gives an affine image of a Gaussian, with mean $tx_1$ and covariance $(1-t)^2I$

$$
X_{t\vert1}=t\,x_1+(1-t)X_0\ \sim\ p_{t\vert1}(\cdot\vert x_1)=\mathcal{N}\big(\cdot\,\vert\,tx_1,\,(1-t)^2I\big).
$$ {#eq-ot-path}

This conditional path satisfies the boundary conditions of @sec-fm-problem. At $t=0$ it is $\mathcal{N}(0,I)=p$, and as $t\to1$ the covariance vanishes and the law tends to $\delta_{x_1}$. Inserting this conditional path into @eq-marginal-path gives the marginal path

$$
p_t(x)=\int\mathcal{N}\big(x\,\vert\,tx_1,(1-t)^2I\big)\,q(x_1)\,\mathrm{d}x_1 ,
$$

which is the law of $tX_1+(1-t)X_0$ with $X_0$ independent of $X_1$.

The conditional velocity is the field whose trajectories are the paths of $X_{t\vert1}$, that is, $\tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}X_{t\vert1}=u_t(X_{t\vert1}\vert x_1)$, so it follows from @eq-velocity-of-flow. Differentiating @eq-ot-flow gives $\dot\psi_t(x_0\vert x_1)=x_1-x_0$, and inverting the flow gives $x_0=(x-tx_1)/(1-t)$, so

$$
u_t(x\vert x_1)=x_1-\frac{x-tx_1}{1-t}=\frac{x_1-x}{1-t}.
$$ {#eq-ot-vel}

This field is defined for $t<1$ only, because of the factor $1/(1-t)$. Along a trajectory $x_t=\psi_t(x_0\vert x_1)$ the velocity is the finite value $x_1-x_0$, so the flow extends continuously to $t=1$, where it maps every $x_0$ to $x_1$ and is therefore not a bijection (@sec-flow-def).

The same field also follows from the Gaussian with time-dependent variance of @sec-ce, now with a moving mean. The law $\mathcal{N}(m_t,\sigma_t^2I)$ is the push-forward of $\mathcal{N}(m_0,\sigma_0^2I)$ by the flow $\psi_t(x)=m_t+(\sigma_t/\sigma_0)(x-m_0)$, so by @eq-velocity-of-flow its velocity is $\dot m_t+(\dot\sigma_t/\sigma_t)(x-m_t)$. With $m_t=tx_1$ and $\sigma_t=1-t$ this is $x_1-(x-tx_1)/(1-t)$, which is the same field. This flow is called the optimal-transport conditional flow, because @eq-ot-flow is the optimal-transport interpolation between $p$ and the point mass $\delta_{x_1}$ [@lipman2024guide, Theorem 5].

### Affine conditional flow matching {#sec-affine}

The straight line @eq-ot-flow, with $\alpha_t=t$ and $\sigma_t=1-t$, is one member of a larger family of paths, the affine interpolations

$$
X_t=\alpha_tX_1+\sigma_tX_0,\qquad \alpha_0=0,\ \sigma_0=1,\qquad \alpha_1=1,\ \sigma_1=0,
$$ {#eq-affine-path}

with differentiable coefficients. In the notation of @eq-ot-flow, the conditional flow is $\psi_t(x_0\vert x_1)=\alpha_tx_1+\sigma_tx_0$. The lecture writes the same interpolation as $\psi_t(x\vert x_0)=a_tx_0+b_tx$ with $a_0=1,b_0=0,a_1=0,b_1=1$, where $x$ takes the role of $x_1$, so that $a_t=\sigma_t$ and $b_t=\alpha_t$. For every path of this family the marginal velocity has three equivalent forms, which the following three steps derive.

**Step 1. The conditional velocity.** Condition on $Z=(X_0,X_1)$. The conditional path is the point mass at $\alpha_tx_1+\sigma_tx_0$, and it is generated by the field $u_t(x\vert x_0,x_1)=\dot\alpha_tx_1+\dot\sigma_tx_0$, which does not depend on $x$, so its flow from the starting point $x_0$ is $x_0+(\alpha_t-\alpha_0)x_1+(\sigma_t-\sigma_0)x_0=\alpha_tx_1+\sigma_tx_0$.

**Step 2. Marginalise.** By @thm-marg, with $Z=(X_0,X_1)$,

$$
u_t(x)=\mathbb{E}\big[\dot\alpha_tX_1+\dot\sigma_tX_0\,\big\vert\,X_t=x\big]
=\dot\alpha_t\,\mathbb{E}[X_1\vert X_t=x]+\dot\sigma_t\,\mathbb{E}[X_0\vert X_t=x].
$$ {#eq-affine-first}

**Step 3. Eliminate one posterior mean.** The two posterior means are not independent, because taking $\mathbb{E}[\,\cdot\,\vert X_t=x]$ of @eq-affine-path gives

$$
x=\alpha_t\,\mathbb{E}[X_1\vert X_t=x]+\sigma_t\,\mathbb{E}[X_0\vert X_t=x].
$$ {#eq-affine-constraint}

Solving @eq-affine-constraint for $\mathbb{E}[X_0\vert X_t=x]=(x-\alpha_t\mathbb{E}[X_1\vert X_t=x])/\sigma_t$ and substituting into @eq-affine-first, and symmetrically for the other mean, gives the two further forms

$$
\begin{aligned}
u_t(x)&=\frac{\dot\sigma_t}{\sigma_t}\,x+\Big[\dot\alpha_t-\alpha_t\frac{\dot\sigma_t}{\sigma_t}\Big]\mathbb{E}[X_1\vert X_t=x]\\
&=\frac{\dot\alpha_t}{\alpha_t}\,x+\Big[\dot\sigma_t-\sigma_t\frac{\dot\alpha_t}{\alpha_t}\Big]\mathbb{E}[X_0\vert X_t=x].
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-affine-forms}

The first form divides by $\sigma_t$, so it holds at the times with $\sigma_t\neq0$, and the second divides by $\alpha_t$, so it holds at the times with $\alpha_t\neq0$. If $\alpha_t>0$ for $t>0$ and $\sigma_t>0$ for $t<1$, as for the straight line and for $\alpha_t=\sin(\pi t/2)$, $\sigma_t=\cos(\pi t/2)$, the first form holds for $t\in[0,1)$ and the second for $t\in(0,1]$, so both hold for $t\in(0,1)$. Three remarks follow.

- The velocity is an affine function of $x$ plus a multiple of one posterior mean, either of the data or of the noise. A network may therefore be trained to predict the data or the noise, and the velocity is then assembled from @eq-affine-forms, so the choice changes only the parametrisation of the same field.
- For the straight line, $\dot\sigma_t/\sigma_t=-1/(1-t)$ and $\dot\alpha_t-\alpha_t\dot\sigma_t/\sigma_t=1+t/(1-t)=1/(1-t)$, so the first form is $u_t(x)=(\mathbb{E}[X_1\vert X_t=x]-x)/(1-t)$ for $t<1$, which is the conditional velocity @eq-ot-vel with the target $x_1$ replaced by its posterior mean. The second form gives $u_t(x)=(x-\mathbb{E}[X_0\vert X_t=x])/t$ for $t>0$.
- Other choices of $(\alpha_t,\sigma_t)$ give other paths. DDPM-type diffusion models use a variance-preserving schedule, which has $\alpha_t^2+\sigma_t^2=1$, and the variance-exploding denoiser of @sec-rf-equiv corresponds to the straight line after the rescaling @eq-scaling. @sec-beyond uses $\alpha_t=\sin(\pi t/2)$, $\sigma_t=\cos(\pi t/2)$ as a comparison.

@tbl-schedulers reads three familiar paths this way. The conditional target is
free of $t$ exactly when $\alpha_t$ and $\sigma_t$ are affine in $t$, which
together with the boundary conditions of @eq-affine-path singles out the
straight line --- and is why the straight line, and not the schedule inherited
from a diffusion model, is the one that makes the regression target as simple
as $X_1-X_0$.

| Path | $\alpha_t$ | $\sigma_t$ | Target $u_t(X_t\vert X_1)$ |
|:-----------|:----|:------|:-------------|
| linear (conditional OT) | $t$ | $1-t$ | $X_1-X_0$ |
| variance preserving | $\sin(\pi t/2)$ | $\cos(\pi t/2)$ | $\tfrac{\pi}{2}\big(\cos(\pi t/2)\,X_1-\sin(\pi t/2)\,X_0\big)$ |
| variance exploding | $1$ | from $\sigma_0\gg1$ to $0$ | $\dot\sigma_t\,X_0$ |

: Three affine paths and their conditional targets. For the variance-exploding path the source is only approximately Gaussian, $q*\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_0^2I)$. {#tbl-schedulers}

### Flow matching in practice {#sec-practice}

The optimal-transport (OT) case gives the following training and sampling procedure, with the noise $x_0$ at $t=0$ and the data $x_1$ at $t=1$.

::: {.callout-note}
## Training and sampling
**Training.**

1. Sample $x_1\sim$ data, $x_0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ and $t\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1]$.
2. Interpolate $x_t=(1-t)x_0+tx_1$.
3. Regress the velocity, $v_\theta(x_t,t)\approx x_1-x_0$.
4. Take a gradient step on the loss.

**Sampling.**

1. Start from $x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ at $t=0$.
2. For $k=0,\dots,K-1$ with $h=1/K$, set $x\leftarrow x+h\,v_\theta(x,kh)$.
3. Return $x$, an approximate sample of the data.
:::

In formulas,

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t,x_0,x_1}\big\lVert v_\theta(x_t,t)-(x_1-x_0)\big\rVert^2,\quad x_t=(1-t)x_0+tx_1,\quad x_{t+h}=x_t+h\,v_\theta(x_t,t).
$$ {#eq-practice}

The regression target $x_1-x_0$ in @eq-practice has a different form from the conditional velocity @eq-ot-vel, which gives $(x_1-X_t)/(1-t)$ at $X_t$, and the two agree sample by sample. If $X_t=tx_1+(1-t)X_0$, then $X_0=(X_t-tx_1)/(1-t)$ is a function of $(X_t,x_1)$, so the target $(x_1-X_t)/(1-t)$ of @eq-ot-vel equals $x_1-X_0$ exactly, not merely on average. This is why the procedure trains on the target $x_1-x_0$, which has no singular factor $1/(1-t)$ at $t\to1$, and why the Gaussian/OT loss of @sec-map is $\lVert u_t^\theta(X_t)-(X_1-X_0)\rVert^2$.

Training is simulation-free, because evaluating the loss needs no ODE solve, only the random triple $(x_0,x_1,t)$. This is the practical advantage over training a continuous normalizing flow by maximum likelihood [@chen2018node], where every training step must integrate the ODE.

@fig-overview shows the four stages of @fig-blueprint for the two-moons data of the example below. Panel (a) shows the noise samples and the data samples, and panel (b) shows samples of the path $p_t$ at three times, which interpolate between the noise cloud and the data. Panel (c) shows the regression targets $x_1-x_0$ at one time, and the arrows at nearby points differ in direction and length, because each target depends on the data point that its noise sample was paired with, so the network can only learn their average. Panel (d) shows that following the learned velocity field from noise samples ends on the two moons.

![The four stages of @fig-blueprint on two moons. Panel (a) shows noise samples $X_0\sim p$ and data samples $X_1\sim q$. Panel (b) shows samples of $X_t=(1-t)X_0+tX_1$ for independent pairs at three times. In panel (c) the network is regressed at $t=0.5$ on the conditional velocity $x_1-x_0$ (arrows, drawn at $1/3.2$ of their length) at each $x_t$ (dots), for 22 pairs. Panel (d) shows trajectories of the learned velocity field from noise (blue) to data (orange), with the data samples of panel (a) in light grey, for the network trained by the listing below.](figures/lec13/yws0322-f0-overview.png){#fig-overview width=100%}

**A runnable example.** The listing below implements this procedure on two moons with one change in the sampling step. Instead of the Euler step it uses the explicit midpoint method, which first computes $x_{\mathrm{mid}}=x+\tfrac h2v_\theta(x,kh)$ and then sets $x\leftarrow x+h\,v_\theta(x_{\mathrm{mid}},(k+\tfrac12)h)$. This method is second-order accurate and needs two network evaluations per step. The listing trains a small network with @eq-practice, prints the loss during training, and evaluates the samples. It needs only the packages `torch`, `numpy` and `scikit-learn`.

```{.python}
import numpy as np
import torch
from torch import nn
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons

torch.manual_seed(0)
moons = make_moons(400_000, noise=0.05, random_state=0)[0]
pool = torch.from_numpy(moons).float()

class Velocity(nn.Module):
    """The velocity network v_theta(x, t)."""
    def __init__(self, hidden=256):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(3, hidden), nn.SiLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden, hidden), nn.SiLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden, hidden), nn.SiLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden, 2))

    def forward(self, x, t):        # x: (B, 2), t: (B, 1)
        return self.net(torch.cat([x, t], dim=1))

v = Velocity()
opt = torch.optim.Adam(v.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

losses = []
for it in range(6000):
    idx = torch.randint(0, len(pool), (4096,))
    x1 = pool[idx]                  # data
    x0 = torch.randn_like(x1)       # noise
    t = torch.rand(4096, 1)
    xt = (1 - t) * x0 + t * x1      # interpolation
    # regression on the target x_1 - x_0
    loss = ((v(xt, t) - (x1 - x0)) ** 2).mean()
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    losses.append(loss.item())
    if (it + 1) % 1000 == 0:
        print(f"iter {it + 1}: {np.mean(losses[-200:]):.4f}")

@torch.no_grad()
def sample(x, K=20):
    # midpoint method with step h = 1/K, started at x
    h = 1.0 / K
    for k in range(K):
        t = torch.full((len(x), 1), k * h)
        x_mid = x + 0.5 * h * v(x, t)
        x = x + h * v(x_mid, t + 0.5 * h)
    return x

def sliced_w1(a, b, n_dir=200):
    d = np.random.default_rng(1).standard_normal((n_dir, 2))
    d /= np.linalg.norm(d, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    dist = [np.abs(np.sort(a @ u) - np.sort(b @ u)).mean()
            for u in d]
    return np.mean(dist)

def show(name, value):
    print(f"{name:22s}{value:.4f}")

N = 20000
noise = torch.randn(N, 2)
gen = sample(noise).numpy()
fresh = pool[torch.randint(0, len(pool), (N,))].numpy()
fresh2 = pool[torch.randint(0, len(pool), (N,))].numpy()
show("loss, last 500 steps", np.mean(losses[-500:]))
show("sliced W1 model/data", sliced_w1(gen, fresh))
show("sliced W1 data/data", sliced_w1(fresh2, fresh))
show("sliced W1 noise/data", sliced_w1(noise.numpy(), fresh))
```

On a CPU (seed 0, about 2.5 minutes) the listing prints the following.

```{.text}
iter 1000: 0.9888
iter 2000: 0.9496
iter 3000: 0.9470
iter 4000: 0.9458
iter 5000: 0.9441
iter 6000: 0.9421
loss, last 500 steps  0.9431
sliced W1 model/data  0.0138
sliced W1 data/data   0.0070
sliced W1 noise/data  0.4425
```

The interpolation `xt` is the line $\alpha_t=t$, $\sigma_t=1-t$ of @eq-affine-path, and the regression target `x1 - x0` is the one of the procedure above. The training loss averages the squared error over the two coordinates as well as over the batch, so it equals $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}/2$. The listing prints its mean over the last $200$ iterations every $1000$ iterations, which is $0.989$ at iteration $1000$, and its mean over the last $500$ iterations at the end. The loss drops quickly and then flattens at $0.943$ (@fig-practice, right). By @thm-cfm twice this value equals $C$ plus the error $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}$ of the network, so a plateau at a positive value is not a failure of the optimiser. The samples at $t=1$ lie on the two moons (left). Their sliced Wasserstein-1 distance to fresh data (the one-dimensional distance averaged over $200$ random directions, for $20000$ samples) is $0.0138$, which is of the same order as the value $0.0070$ between two independent data sets of the same size and far below the value $0.4425$ for the initial noise.

![Training the velocity field with the procedure of @eq-practice on two moons. The left panels show samples of the learned ODE at $t=0,\,0.25,\,0.5,\,0.75$ (blue) and at $t=1$ (orange), the last together with fresh data (grey). The right panel shows the printed training loss, which is $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}/2$ and flattens at $0.943$ and not at zero, as @thm-cfm predicts. The sliced Wasserstein-1 distance to fresh data is $0.0138$, compared with $0.0070$ between two data sets and $0.4425$ for the initial noise.](figures/lec13/yws0322-f8-training-example.png){#fig-practice width=100%}

**Summary.** The lecture emphasizes two facts as the conclusion of the flow matching part.

1. The regression target is simple. A noise sample $x_0$ and a data sample $x_1$ can be drawn independently, and the target is their difference $x_1-x_0$, which does not depend on $t$ for the pair and needs no ODE solve, so training is simulation-free.
2. The final loss @eq-practice is a function of samples only. The marginal velocity, the marginalization theorem (@thm-marg) and the gradient equivalence (@thm-cfm) are needed to justify the loss, but the loss itself needs only $x_0$, $x_1$ and $t$ (through $x_t$), so training needs only samples from the data and from the noise.

It is worth saying which half of the procedure the word *simulation-free*
describes. Training is simulation-free: no ODE is solved and no divergence or
density is evaluated. Sampling is not --- generation still integrates the
learned field, as the loop above does, and @sec-timegrid is about how to spend
those steps.

The target is also what separates this from score matching, which is the
comparison @tbl-targets makes: a score target depends on the corruption process
and carries its scale, while the flow target does not.

| Model | Corruption of the data $x$ | Conditional target |
|:-------------|:--------------|:------------|
| score matching, variance exploding | $x+\sigma_t\,\epsilon$ | $-\epsilon/\sigma_t$ |
| score matching, variance preserving | $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon$ | $-\epsilon/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}$ |
| flow matching, linear path, any coupling | $(1-t)\,x_0+t\,x_1$ | $x_1-x_0$ |

: Regression targets, with $\bar\alpha_t$ the cumulative product of the DDPM schedule. {#tbl-targets}

## Rectified flow and its equivalence with diffusion {#sec-rf}

The straight-line path of the training example above is the path of rectified flow, and this section relates the training objective of rectified flow to the denoising objective of a diffusion model. A noisy sample of a diffusion model is a data point plus added noise, so the comparison is easiest with data at $t=0$ and noise at $t=1$, which reverses the time convention used in the rest of the note (@tbl-flow-notation-rf). The comparison also needs a change of the time variable. The noise level $s\in(0,\infty)$ of the denoising loss is mapped to $t=s/(1+s)\in(0,1)$, and with it the denoising loss becomes the rectified-flow loss @eq-rf-loss up to a positive time weight and a different distribution of $t$ (@sec-rf-equiv).

**Convention switch.** Here $x_0\sim p_0$ is a data point and $x_1\sim p_1=\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ is noise, and a model generates by integrating from $t=1$ down to $t=0$. Although the labels change, the two conventions describe the same straight-line path. The path $X_t=tX_1+(1-t)X_0$ of the earlier sections, with $X_1$ data, becomes the path $x_t=(1-t)x_0+tx_1$ used below after renaming data to $x_0$, noise to $x_1$ and time $t$ to $1-t$. Since time runs in the opposite direction, velocities change sign. If $u^{\mathrm{I}}_t$ denotes a velocity field of the earlier sections and $v_t$ the corresponding field of this section, then $u^{\mathrm{I}}_t(x)=-v_{1-t}(x)$. Within this section the letters $v$ and $u$ both denote velocities in the reversed convention, as on the lecture slides. The reversed convention is used only in this section.

### Rectified flow and the linear conditional flow {#sec-rf-linear}

Rectified flow uses the simplest conditional flow of @sec-affine. Conditioned on the data point $x_0$, it maps linearly to the noise point,

$$
\psi_t(x\vert x_0)=a_tx_0+b_tx,\qquad a_t=1-t,\quad b_t=t,
$$ {#eq-rf-flow}

where $x$ denotes the noise sample $x_1$ (indeed $\psi_0=x_0$ and $\psi_1=x$). Its conditional velocity is the constant

$$
v_t(x_t\vert x_0)=\dot\psi_t(x_1\vert x_0)=\dot a_tx_0+\dot b_tx_1=x_1-x_0,\qquad x_t=(1-t)x_0+tx_1 .
$$ {#eq-rf-vel}

The training problem is then the regression

$$
\min_\theta\ \mathbb{E}_{t,\,x_0\sim p_0,\,x_t\sim p_{t\vert0}(\cdot\vert x_0)}\big\lVert v_t(x_t\vert x_0)-v^\theta_t(x_t)\big\rVert^2=\min_\theta\ \mathbb{E}_{t,\,x_0,\,x_1}\big\lVert v_t^\theta(x_t)-(x_1-x_0)\big\rVert^2 ,
$$ {#eq-rf-loss}

which is the CFM loss of the practical procedure, written in the reversed convention of this section. The two sides agree because their targets are the same random variable. Given $x_0$ and $x_t$ the noise point is determined, $x_1=(x_t-(1-t)x_0)/t$, so $v_t(x_t\vert x_0)=(x_t-x_0)/t=x_1-x_0$.

### 1-rectified flow {#sec-rf-def}

The loss @eq-rf-loss involves pairs $(x_0,x_1)$ of a data point and a noise point, and 1-rectified flow (1-RF) is the case in which the pair is drawn independently. It uses the following objects

$$
p^0_{01}=p_0\otimes p_1,\qquad p_t(x\vert x_0,x_1)=\delta\big(x-((1-t)x_0+tx_1)\big),\qquad u_t(x\vert x_0,x_1)=x_1-x_0 .
$$ {#eq-1rf}

Here $p^0_{01}$ is the independent coupling of a data point with a noise point, that is, $p^0_{01}(x_0,x_1)=p_0(x_0)\,p_1(x_1)$, and the superscript $0$ marks it as the starting coupling (couplings produced by repeating the procedure belong to ReFlow, which is outside the scope of this note). The conditional path $p_t(x\vert x_0,x_1)$ is the pair-conditioned path of the last row of @tbl-conditioning, written there as $p_{t\vert0,1}$ in the earlier time convention. We first check that $u_t(x\vert x_0,x_1)$ generates $p_t(x\vert x_0,x_1)$. Since the conditional velocity is the constant $x_1-x_0$, its flow from the starting point $x_0$ is

$$
x_t=x_0+\int_0^tu_s(x\vert x_0,x_1)\,\mathrm{d}s=x_0+\int_0^t(x_1-x_0)\,\mathrm{d}s=x_0+t(x_1-x_0)=(1-t)x_0+tx_1,
$$

which is the support point of the delta path, so $u_t(x\vert x_0,x_1)$ generates $p_t(x\vert x_0,x_1)$. By the marginalization theorem (@thm-marg with $Z=(X_0,X_1)$) the marginal velocity is then $u_t(x)=\mathbb{E}[x_1-x_0\vert x_t=x]$, and by @thm-cfm it is the minimiser of the regression on $x_1-x_0$ in @eq-rf-loss.

### Equivalence of 1-RF and diffusion {#sec-rf-equiv}

This section shows how the denoising objective of a diffusion model is transformed into the rectified-flow loss by a change of variables and a time weight, and that the two objectives have corresponding minimisers. The derivation starts from the diffusion objective and transforms it into the rectified-flow loss in four steps.

**The diffusion side.** A denoising diffusion model, in the form used by @karras2022edm, is a denoiser $D_s(\cdot;\theta)$ that, given the noisy input $x_0+s\,\epsilon$ at noise level $s$, predicts the clean $x_0$. The denoising objective is

$$
\min_\theta\ \mathbb{E}_{s\in(0,\infty)}\,\mathbb{E}_{x_0\sim p_0}\,\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)}\big\lVert x_0-D_s(x_0+s\,\epsilon;\theta)\big\rVert^2 ,
$$ {#eq-flow-dsm}

with a weighting over the noise level $s$ that is left unspecified. Its ideal solution is the posterior mean $D_s^\ast(x)=\mathbb{E}[x_0\vert x_0+s\epsilon=x]$. The lecture calls this objective denoising score matching [@vincent2011], because it is the score matching objective for a particular parametrisation of the score. Write $\tilde x=x_0+s\epsilon$ and the score network as $(D_s(\tilde x;\theta)-\tilde x)/s^2$. The score of the noised data given $x_0$ is $\nabla_{\tilde x}\log\mathcal{N}(\tilde x\vert x_0,s^2I)=-(\tilde x-x_0)/s^2$, so the squared score error equals $s^{-4}\lVert x_0-D_s(\tilde x;\theta)\rVert^2$. The two objectives therefore differ only by the factor $s^{-4}$, which belongs to the weighting over $s$.

**Step 1. Name the noise.** Write the Gaussian noise as $x_1:=\epsilon\sim p_1=\mathcal{N}(0,I)$. Then $(x_0,x_1)$ is a draw from the independent coupling $p^0_{01}=p_0\otimes\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ of @eq-1rf, and @eq-flow-dsm becomes $\min_\theta\mathbb{E}_{s}\mathbb{E}_{(x_0,x_1)\sim p^0_{01}}\lVert x_0-D_s(x_0+s\,x_1;\theta)\rVert^2$.

**Step 2. Change the time variable.** Put $t=s/(1+s)$, equivalently $s=t/(1-t)$, which maps $s\in(0,\infty)$ onto $t\in(0,1)$. Then, with $x_t=(1-t)x_0+tx_1$ the point of the rectified path,

$$
x_0+s\,x_1=x_0+\frac{t}{1-t}\,x_1=\frac{(1-t)x_0+tx_1}{1-t}=\frac{x_t}{1-t}.
$$ {#eq-scaling}

So the noisy input of the denoiser is the rectified-flow point multiplied by $1/(1-t)$. Panel (a) of @fig-timeconv shows that $s=t/(1-t)$ maps $t\in(0,1)$ onto all noise levels $s\in(0,\infty)$, with $s\to\infty$ as $t\to1$. Panel (b) shows for one pair $(x_0,x_1)$ that $x_t$ and $x_0+s\,x_1$ lie on the same ray from the origin and differ only by the factor $1/(1-t)$, which is $2$ at $t=0.5$ and $5$ at $t=0.8$. The objective is therefore

$$
\min_\theta\ \mathbb{E}_{t\in(0,1)}\,\mathbb{E}_{(x_0,x_1)\sim p^0_{01}}\,\mathbb{E}_{x_t\sim p_t(\cdot\vert x_0,x_1)}\Big\lVert x_0-D_{t/(1-t)}\Big(\frac{x_t}{1-t};\theta\Big)\Big\rVert^2 .
$$ {#eq-flow-dsm-t}

(The change of variable also turns the weighting over $s$ into a weighting over $t\in(0,1)$.)

![The change of variable of the equivalence derivation, with $x_0$ data and $x_1$ noise as in @sec-rf. Panel (a) shows the noise level $s=t/(1-t)$ as a function of the rectified-flow time $t$. Panel (b) shows, for one pair $(x_0,x_1)$, the rectified-flow path $x_t=(1-t)x_0+tx_1$ (blue segment) and the noise-added path $x_0+s\,x_1$ (orange ray). The point $x_0+s\,x_1$ equals $x_t/(1-t)$, so it lies on the ray from the origin through $x_t$ (dotted), and the two paths differ by a radial rescaling by the factor $1/(1-t)$, which is $2$ at $t=0.5$ and $5$ at $t=0.8$. The marked points are $t=0.5\leftrightarrow s=1$ and $t=0.8\leftrightarrow s=4$.](figures/lec13/yws0322-f5-time-conventions.png){#fig-timeconv width=100%}

**Step 3. Turn the denoiser error into a velocity error.** Since $x_t-x_0=(1-t)x_0+tx_1-x_0=t(x_1-x_0)$, the error of the denoiser can be rewritten in terms of the conditional velocity $x_1-x_0$. Abbreviate $D=D_{t/(1-t)}(x_t/(1-t);\theta)$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_0-D&=(x_0-x_t)+(x_t-D)=-t\Big[(x_1-x_0)-t^{-1}(x_t-D)\Big],\\
\lVert x_0-D\rVert^2&=t^2\,\Big\lVert(x_1-x_0)-t^{-1}(x_t-D)\Big\rVert^2 .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-t2}

This form suggests defining a velocity network from the denoiser by

$$
u_t(x;\theta):=t^{-1}\Big\{x-D_{t/(1-t)}\Big(\frac{x}{1-t};\theta\Big)\Big\},\qquad t\in(0,1).
$$ {#eq-vel-from-denoiser}

The bracket in @eq-t2 is then $(x_1-x_0)-u_t(x_t;\theta)=u_t(x_t\vert x_0,x_1)-u_t(x_t;\theta)$, and the objective becomes

$$
\min_\theta\ \mathbb{E}_{t}\Big[t^2\ \mathbb{E}_{(x_0,x_1),\,x_t}\big\lVert u_t(x_t\vert x_0,x_1)-u_t(x_t;\theta)\big\rVert^2\Big].
$$ {#eq-flow-dsm-vel}

**Step 4. Drop the weight.** The problem is separable with respect to $t$, so the factor $t^2$ can be removed, which leaves $\min_\theta\mathbb{E}_{t}\mathbb{E}\lVert u_t(x_t\vert x_0,x_1)-u_t(x_t;\theta)\rVert^2$, the 1-rectified-flow matching loss of @eq-rf-loss. The justification is that, if the network can be chosen freely at each $t$, the objective is a sum (an integral) of independent terms, one per $t$, each multiplied by a weight, and a weight that is positive for almost every $t$ does not change where a term is minimised. This applies to $t^2$, which is positive on $(0,1)$, and also to the weighting over $t$ that the change of variable inherits from the weighting over $s$, which can therefore be replaced by the uniform distribution of $t$ used in @eq-rf-loss. The inherited weighting is positive for almost every $t$ if and only if the weighting over $s$ is positive for almost every $s$, because $s\mapsto t$ is a diffeomorphism of $(0,\infty)$ onto $(0,1)$, so the argument assumes that the weighting over $s$ is positive for almost every $s$.

**What exactly is equivalent.** Because Step 4 relies on the separability argument, the equivalence needs a precise statement. Two statements hold.

1. **The minimisers correspond.** The minimiser of the rectified-flow loss is $u_t^\ast(x)=\mathbb{E}[x_1-x_0\vert x_t=x]$. Because $x_1-x_0=(x_t-x_0)/t$,
$$
u_t^\ast(x)=t^{-1}\big(x-\mathbb{E}[x_0\vert x_t=x]\big)=t^{-1}\Big(x-D^\ast_{t/(1-t)}\Big(\frac{x}{1-t}\Big)\Big),
$$
using that conditioning on $x_t$ is the same as conditioning on $x_t/(1-t)=x_0+s\,x_1$ (@eq-scaling) and that $D_s^\ast(y)=\mathbb{E}[x_0\vert x_0+sx_1=y]$. This is @eq-vel-from-denoiser applied to the ideal denoiser, without any appeal to the separability argument.
2. **The objectives differ by a positive time weight.** @eq-flow-dsm-vel contains the factor $t^2$ (and a different distribution of $t$, inherited from that of $s$), whereas the rectified-flow loss does not. For a network of finite capacity, trained by stochastic gradient descent, the weighting determines how much each time contributes to the loss, so the two training runs are not identical. What coincides is the population minimiser and the change of coordinates between the two networks.

**The inverse formula.** The relation @eq-vel-from-denoiser can be inverted, so that a denoiser is obtained from a velocity network. Put $t=s/(1+s)$ and $x=x_t(1+s)$, i.e. $x_t=x/(1+s)$ and $x_t/(1-t)=x$. Then @eq-vel-from-denoiser gives $D_s(x;\theta)=x_t-t\,u_t(x_t;\theta)$, that is,

$$
D_s(x;\theta)=(1+s)^{-1}\Big\{x-s\,u_{s/(1+s)}\Big(\frac{x}{1+s};\theta\Big)\Big\},\qquad s\in(0,\infty),
$$ {#eq-denoiser-from-vel}

which is the inverse relation of @eq-vel-from-denoiser. The two formulas let a velocity network and a denoiser be converted into each other with no change of parameters, so the 1-RF velocity can be computed from a diffusion denoiser and a diffusion denoiser can be computed from the 1-RF velocity.

### Where the trajectories go {#sec-rf-ode}

The equivalence above concerns training objectives. The same change of variable also relates the sampling trajectories, as the following derivation shows. Let $x_t$ follow the rectified-flow ODE $\dot x_t=u_t(x_t)$ with $u_t$ given by @eq-vel-from-denoiser (in this subsection $x_t$ denotes this ODE trajectory and not the point $(1-t)x_0+tx_1$ of a pair), and set $s=t/(1-t)$, $y=x_t/(1-t)=(1+s)x_t$. Since $t=s/(1+s)$ we have $\mathrm{d}t/\mathrm{d}s=(1+s)^{-2}$, and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}s}&=x_t+(1+s)\,\dot x_t\,\frac{\mathrm{d}t}{\mathrm{d}s}=x_t+\frac{u_t(x_t)}{1+s}
=x_t+\frac{x_t-D_s(y)}{s}\\
&=\frac{y}{1+s}\Big(1+\frac1s\Big)-\frac{D_s(y)}{s}=\frac{y-D_s(y)}{s},
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ve-ode}

using $u_t(x_t)=t^{-1}(x_t-D_s(y))=\frac{1+s}{s}(x_t-D_s(y))$ and $x_t=y/(1+s)$.
