The right-hand side $(y-D_s(y))/s$ is the probability-flow ODE of the variance-exploding diffusion in the parametrisation of @karras2022edm and @sde with noise level $\sigma=s$. So the integral curves of the rectified-flow field are the diffusion probability-flow curves, rescaled by $1-t$ and reparametrised by $s=t/(1-t)$, which gives the same trajectories expressed in different variables. What differs in practice is the time grid on which a solver takes its steps (a uniform grid in $t$ is a very non-uniform grid in $s$) and which noise levels the loss emphasises.

The correspondence holds step by step and not only in the limit, which is what
makes it usable.

::: {#prp-ddim}
## An Euler step of the flow is a DDIM step
Let $x'=x+(t'-t)\,u_t(x)$ be one Euler step of the rectified-flow ODE with
$u_t$ as in @eq-vel-from-denoiser, and write $y=x/(1-t)$, $y'=x'/(1-t')$,
$s=t/(1-t)$ and $s'=t'/(1-t')$. Then

$$
y'=y+\frac{s'-s}{s}\big(y-D_s(y)\big)=D_s(y)+\frac{s'}{s}\big(y-D_s(y)\big).
$$ {#eq-ddim}
:::

::: {.proof}
By @eq-vel-from-denoiser, $u_t(x)=t^{-1}(x-D_s(y))$, so
$x'=x+(t'-t)\,(x-D_s(y))/t$. Divide by $1-t'$ and use $x=(1-t)y$ together with

$$
s'-s=\frac{t'}{1-t'}-\frac{t}{1-t}=\frac{t'-t}{(1-t')(1-t)},
$$

which gives $y'=(s'/s)\,y-\big((s'-s)/s\big)D_s(y)$. Collecting the two terms
in $y$ gives the first form of @eq-ddim and collecting the two in $D_s(y)$ the
second.
:::

The second form of @eq-ddim is the deterministic DDIM update in its
variance-exploding parametrisation: denoise to $D_s(y)$, then add back the
fraction $s'/s$ of the noise that was removed. So an Euler sampler of 1-RF on a
grid $1>t_K>\dots>t_0=0$ returns exactly what DDIM returns on the noise levels
$s_k=t_k/(1-t_k)$, given the same optimal network and the matching starting
point $x=y/(1+s_K)$. The two models are therefore not merely related at their
optima; with the grids in correspondence, moving from one to the other changes
nothing at all. What is left to choose is where the steps go, which is
@sec-timegrid.

### Where the steps go {#sec-timegrid}

@prp-ddim leaves the time grid as the only difference between a flow sampler
and a diffusion sampler, so it is worth seeing how strongly the change of
variable deforms it. From $t=s/(1+s)$,

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}t}{\mathrm{d}s}=\frac{1}{(1+s)^{2}},
$$ {#eq-dtds}

so flow time saturates as the noise level grows. Every level above $s=9$, an
unbounded range, is squeezed into $0.9<t<1$, and the local step
$\mathrm{d}t=\mathrm{d}s/(1+s)^2$ is $81^2=6561$ times shorter at $s=80$ than
at $s=0$. Read the other way, a grid uniform in $t$ with $K=10$ steps visits the
noise levels $\infty,\ 9,\ 4,\ 2.33,\ 1.5,\ 1,\ 0.67,\ 0.43,\ 0.25,\ 0.11,\ 0$:
its first step crosses every level above $9$ at once, and half of its steps lie
below $s=1$, where the noise is weaker than the data.

Standard diffusion schedules lean the other way. Of the $1000$ steps of the
linear-$\beta$ DDPM schedule, $34\%$ lie at $t>0.9$ and $74\%$ at $t>0.5$; of
the $18$ levels of the EDM schedule [@karras2022edm, eq. (5)], $6$ lie at
$t>0.9$ and $11$ at $t>0.5$. (For a variance-preserving model the corresponding
level is $s=\sqrt{(1-\bar\alpha_t)/\bar\alpha_t}$, since
$x_t/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}=x_0+s\,\epsilon$.) Since $\log s$ is the logit of $t$,
the log-normal noise levels used to train EDM are logit-normal flow times,
which is the distribution found best for training rectified flows at scale
[@esser2024sd3].

![One ODE in two coordinate systems, for the Gaussian-mixture target of @sec-gm. (a) Diffusion variables $(s,y)$. (b) Rectified-flow variables $t=s/(1+s)$, $x=y/(1+s)$. The vertical lines mark a ten-step grid that is uniform in $t$; in the diffusion variables of (a) the same grid crowds towards small $s$. (c) The grid points of four ten-step samplers placed on the flow-time axis. Blue and orange distinguish the two modes.](figures/lec13/Jiwon-ch-time-reparam.png){#fig-timegrid width=100%}

@fig-timegrid shows the compression. In the diffusion variables of panel (a) the
trajectories fan out without bound and a grid uniform in flow time crowds
towards small $s$; in the flow variables of panel (b) the same trajectories are
confined to the unit interval, where that grid is uniform. Panel (c) places four
ten-step samplers on one axis: DDIM puts $8$ of its $11$ points at $t>0.5$ and
$4$ at $t>0.9$, EDM crowds at both ends, and a grid uniform in $s$ has all but
its last point at $t>0.88$.

Two caveats keep the conclusion honest. The grid is not intrinsic to either
model --- a diffusion sampler may use the grid induced by uniform $t$, and the
EDM schedule was designed for a second-order solver on images --- and whatever
advantage a uniform flow-time grid has comes from the time parametrisation
rather than from straightness, since the trajectories of 1-RF are curved in
both coordinate systems (@fig-lines).

### Diffusion versus flow matching {#sec-diff-vs-fm}

With the equivalence established, @tbl-diff-vs-fm compares the two families (after the closing table of the lecture).

| | Diffusion (score-based) | Flow matching / rectified flow |
|:------------|:--------------------------|:--------------------------|
| Path | fixed noising SDE, $x_t=\alpha_tx+\sigma_t\varepsilon$ | designed interpolation, $x_t=(1-t)x_0+tx_1$ |
| Network predicts | noise $\varepsilon$, score, or denoiser $D$ | velocity $u_t$ ($=x_1-x_0$ conditionally) |
| Sampler | reverse SDE or probability-flow ODE | ODE solver (Euler, Heun, ...) |
| Trajectories | curved | straight conditionally and straighter after ReFlow |
| Relation | for Gaussian paths velocity, score and denoiser are interchangeable (Tweedie) | 1-RF is diffusion up to reparametrisation |
| Examples | DDPM, EDM, Stable Diffusion 1.x and XL | Stable Diffusion 3, FLUX.1 |

: Comparison of diffusion and flow matching. {#tbl-diff-vs-fm}

Each row is developed in the following places. The paths are in @sec-affine and @sec-rf-linear, what the network predicts is in @sec-rf-equiv and @sec-flow-score, the samplers are in @sec-euler and @sec-rf-ode, the trajectories are in @fig-lines, and the relation row is in @sec-flow-score and @sec-rf-equiv.

## Velocity, score and denoiser {#sec-flow-score}

The "Relation" row of the table says that for Gaussian paths the velocity, the score and the denoiser determine each other. We derive this in the convention of @sec-affine, with noise at $t=0$, so $X_t=\alpha_tX_1+\sigma_tX_0$ with $X_0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ independent of the data $X_1$. The derivation needs one additional result, Tweedie's formula, which expresses the score through a posterior mean. The formulas below hold at the times with $\alpha_t\neq0$ and $\sigma_t>0$, which is $t\in(0,1)$ if $\alpha_t>0$ for $t>0$ and $\sigma_t>0$ for $t<1$ as in @sec-affine.

**Tweedie's formula for the noise.** Let $p_t$ be the density of $X_t$, so that

$$
p_t(x)=\int\mathcal{N}(x\vert\alpha_tx_1,\sigma_t^2I)\,q(x_1)\,\mathrm{d}x_1 .
$$

Differentiating the Gaussian kernel and dividing by $p_t(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla p_t(x)&=\int-\frac{x-\alpha_tx_1}{\sigma_t^2}\,\mathcal{N}(x\vert\alpha_tx_1,\sigma_t^2I)\,q(x_1)\,\mathrm{d}x_1,\\
\nabla\log p_t(x)&=-\frac{1}{\sigma_t^2}\,\mathbb{E}\big[X_t-\alpha_tX_1\,\big\vert\,X_t=x\big]=-\frac{1}{\sigma_t}\,\mathbb{E}[X_0\vert X_t=x],
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-flow-tweedie}

because $X_t-\alpha_tX_1=\sigma_tX_0$ and $\nabla p_t/p_t$ is the posterior average of the kernel's score. This is Tweedie's formula [@efron2011].

**Velocity in terms of the score.** The second form of @eq-affine-forms contains the same posterior mean $\mathbb{E}[X_0\vert X_t=x]$. Inserting $\mathbb{E}[X_0\vert X_t=x]=-\sigma_t\nabla\log p_t(x)$ into it gives

$$
u_t(x)=\frac{\dot\alpha_t}{\alpha_t}\,x+\Big(\frac{\sigma_t^2\dot\alpha_t}{\alpha_t}-\sigma_t\dot\sigma_t\Big)\nabla\log p_t(x).
$$ {#eq-vel-score}

For the OT line $\alpha_t=t$, $\sigma_t=1-t$ the coefficient of the score is $(1-t)^2/t+(1-t)=(1-t)/t$, so

$$
u_t(x)=\frac{x+(1-t)\,\nabla\log p_t(x)}{t}.
$$ {#eq-vel-score-ot}

**Check.** If the data is the single point $X_1=0$, then $X_t=(1-t)X_0$, $p_t=\mathcal{N}(0,(1-t)^2I)$ and $\nabla\log p_t(x)=-x/(1-t)^2$. @eq-vel-score-ot gives $u_t(x)=\big(x-x/(1-t)\big)/t=-x/(1-t)$, which is the velocity $(\dot\sigma_t/\sigma_t)x$ of the Gaussian with time-dependent variance of @sec-ce.

**The denoiser.** The posterior mean of the data, which is the ideal denoiser, follows from @eq-affine-constraint and @eq-flow-tweedie, and it is $\mathbb{E}[X_1\vert X_t=x]=(x-\sigma_t\mathbb{E}[X_0\vert X_t=x])/\alpha_t=(x+\sigma_t^2\nabla\log p_t(x))/\alpha_t$. Velocity, score and denoiser are therefore related by affine maps with known time-dependent coefficients. These maps can be inverted when the coefficients are finite and nonzero, that is, when $\alpha_t\neq0$, $\sigma_t>0$ and the coefficient of the score in @eq-vel-score, $\sigma_t(\sigma_t\dot\alpha_t-\dot\sigma_t\alpha_t)/\alpha_t$, is nonzero. The last condition means $\sigma_t\dot\alpha_t\neq\dot\sigma_t\alpha_t$. It holds for $t\in(0,1)$ if $\dot\alpha_t>0>\dot\sigma_t$ there, because then $\alpha_t$ and $\sigma_t$ are positive and $\sigma_t\dot\alpha_t-\dot\sigma_t\alpha_t>0$, and for the OT line the coefficient is $(1-t)/t$. Under these conditions a network trained for any one of the three gives the other two, and the only further requirement is a choice of the time parametrisation $(\alpha_t,\sigma_t)$.

**No normalisation constant.** Velocity matching and score matching differ in how the normalisation of $p_t$ enters. A score $\nabla\log p_t$ determines $p_t$ only up to a multiplicative constant, which is fixed by the condition $\int p_t\,\mathrm{d}x=1$. Matching a velocity field involves no such constant, for three reasons. First, the regression target $u_t(x\vert z)$ is a vector field with an actual value at each point, not the gradient of an unnormalised log-density. Second, the path is not computed from the velocity at each point separately. It is the push-forward of $p_0$ along the flow of $u_t$ (@eq-flow-pushforward), and by @thm-ce total mass is conserved, so the normalisation of $p_t$ follows from that of $p_0$. Third, for Gaussian paths the velocity is an affine function of the score with a coefficient that is nonzero on $(0,1)$ under the conditions above (@eq-vel-score), so matching $u_t$ determines $\nabla\log p_t$ uniquely. In addition, the conditional and marginal objectives of @thm-cfm are related in the same way as in denoising score matching [@vincent2011], since the regression target is a conditional quantity and its conditional expectation is the marginal one.

## Additional results {#sec-beyond}

This section has two aims. The first is to give the exact marginal velocity for the one-dimensional examples of the figures, so that the figures and the numbers quoted from them are exact and reproducible. The second is one additional experiment, which tests whether straight conditional paths allow sampling with few Euler steps.

### Exact velocities for a Gaussian-mixture target {#sec-gm}

Let $X_0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ be independent of $X_1\sim\sum_kw_k\,\mathcal{N}(m_k,S^2)$, and take any affine path $X_t=\alpha_tX_1+\sigma_tX_0$. Given the mixture component $k$, the pair $(X_1,X_t)$ is jointly Gaussian with $\operatorname{Var}(X_t)=v_t:=\alpha_t^2S^2+\sigma_t^2$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_t)=\alpha_tS^2$, so

$$
\mathbb{E}[X_1\vert X_t=x,k]=m_k+\frac{\alpha_tS^2}{v_t}\,(x-\alpha_tm_k),\qquad
\gamma_k(x)=\frac{w_k\,\mathcal{N}(x\vert\alpha_tm_k,v_t)}{\sum_jw_j\,\mathcal{N}(x\vert\alpha_tm_j,v_t)},
$$ {#eq-gm-posterior}

where $\gamma_k(x)$ is the posterior probability of component $k$ given $X_t=x$. Hence $\mathbb{E}[X_1\vert X_t=x]=\sum_k\gamma_k(x)\,\mathbb{E}[X_1\vert X_t=x,k]$, and inserting this into the first form of @eq-affine-forms gives the marginal velocity in closed form,

$$
u_t(x)=\frac{\dot\sigma_t}{\sigma_t}\,x+\Big[\dot\alpha_t-\alpha_t\frac{\dot\sigma_t}{\sigma_t}\Big]\sum_k\gamma_k(x)\Big(m_k+\frac{\alpha_tS^2}{v_t}(x-\alpha_tm_k)\Big).
$$ {#eq-gm-vel}

For the OT line ($\alpha_t=t$, $\sigma_t=1-t$) this is $u_t(x)=(\mathbb{E}[X_1\vert X_t=x]-x)/(1-t)$. @fig-lines, @fig-thm4 and @fig-fewstep use this formula with $m_k=\pm1.5$, $S=0.35$, $w_k=\tfrac12$. As a check of the formula (and of @eq-affine-first, from which it comes) the closed form was compared with a Monte Carlo estimate of $\mathbb{E}[\dot\alpha_tX_1+\dot\sigma_tX_0\vert X_t=x]$ in bins of $x$ ($4\times10^6$ to $6\times10^6$ samples). The largest standardised deviation was $z=2.96$ over $32$ bins for the OT path at $t=0.5$, and at most $z=3.07$ over $40$ bins for the OT and the variance-preserving path at $t=0.3$ and $t=0.7$, which is within the range expected for a correct formula over that many bins.

### A few-step sampling comparison {#sec-fewstep}

It is often suggested that straight paths need few solver steps, and @tbl-diff-vs-fm qualifies this, since the trajectories are straight only conditionally and become straighter after ReFlow. With exact velocities this can be measured directly. On the mixture above we compare $K$ Euler steps of size $1/K$ for two paths with the same endpoints, namely the OT line and the variance-preserving (VP) path $\alpha_t=\sin(\pi t/2)$, $\sigma_t=\cos(\pi t/2)$ (whose velocity is @eq-gm-vel with those coefficients). The metric is the one-dimensional Wasserstein-1 distance between $2\times10^4$ generated samples and $2\times10^4$ fresh data samples, and two independent data samples are $0.0082$ apart, which is the noise floor. These values come from one draw of the samples. Over 40 further draws the distance between two data samples ranged from $0.005$ to $0.040$ (median $0.012$), mainly because the fraction of samples in each mixture component varies between draws, so values near the floor are accurate only to about $0.01$.

| Steps $K$ | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 | 16 | 32 | 64 | 128 |
|:-------------|:------:|:------:|:------:|:------:|:------:|:------:|:------:|:------:|
| OT path | 1.4995 | 0.5597 | 0.2192 | 0.1133 | 0.0599 | 0.0341 | 0.0222 | 0.0172 |
| VP path | 0.7192 | 0.2476 | 0.0493 | 0.0225 | 0.0157 | 0.0132 | 0.0127 | 0.0129 |

: Wasserstein-1 distance between $K$-step Euler samples and data, for one draw of the samples (noise floor $0.0082$). {#tbl-fewstep}

![Euler sampling with $K$ steps for the OT path and a variance-preserving (VP) path on the exact one-dimensional mixture of @fig-lines, measured by the Wasserstein-1 distance to fresh data (log-log axes, twelve values of $K$, of which @tbl-fewstep lists eight). The dashed line is the distance between two independent data samples of the same draw. In this example the VP path is the better of the two at every $K$ tested.](figures/lec13/yws0322-f7-few-step-sampling.png){#fig-fewstep width=70%}

@fig-fewstep plots these distances on logarithmic axes, for the values of @tbl-fewstep and four further values of $K$. Both distances generally decrease as $K$ grows. The VP distance fluctuates slightly around a plateau of about $0.013$ from $K=32$ on ($0.0132$, $0.0127$ and $0.0129$ at $K=32$, $64$ and $128$), and the OT distance is still decreasing at $K=128$ ($0.0172$). The VP path is better at every $K$ tested, the opposite of what the statement that straight paths need few solver steps suggests. In five further draws with other seeds it was again better at every $K$, except at $K=128$ in one draw, where both distances are at the noise level. The reason is visible in @fig-lines. The conditional OT paths are straight, but the marginal flow that the sampler integrates is not (middle panel there). Its trajectories first move towards the centre and then separate into the two components of the data distribution. The effect is largest for a single step. At $t=0$ the OT velocity is $u_0(x)=\mathbb{E}[X_1]-x=-x$, so one Euler step sends every sample to $0$, the mean of the data, and the distance equals $\mathbb{E}\lvert X_1\rvert\approx1.50$, as the table shows. This does not contradict @tbl-diff-vs-fm, because the paths are straight only conditionally and become straighter after ReFlow, which is outside the scope of this note. The result shows that straight conditional paths do not imply straight sampling trajectories for a model trained on independent couplings. A second, smaller example separates straightness from optimal
transport itself. Let the source be uniform on $\{-1,1\}$ and the target uniform
on $\{-2,2\}$. The order-preserving coupling pairs $(-1,-2)$ and $(1,2)$, with
mean squared displacement $1$; the crossed coupling pairs $(-1,2)$ and $(1,-2)$,
with mean squared displacement $9$. Both consist of straight segments, and only
the first minimises quadratic transport cost. Straightness is a property of the
segments, optimality a property of the pairing, and it is the pairing that
ReFlow changes. The comparison uses a small synthetic setting with exact velocities, a uniform time grid and one data distribution. It therefore says nothing about trained image models, and other time grids or schedules would change the numbers.

## Further reading {#sec-flow-further-reading}

The main reference is the Flow Matching Guide and Code by @lipman2024guide. Its Sections 3 and 4 correspond to this note. Section 3.5 covers the continuity equation, Section 4.4 general conditioning and marginalization, Section 4.5 the loss and @thm-cfm, and Sections 4.7 and 4.8 optimal-transport and affine conditional flows. The original flow-matching papers are @lipman2023fm, @liu2023rf for rectified flow and @albergo2023si for stochastic interpolants. For the diffusion side see @karras2022edm, whose denoiser parametrisation is used in @sec-rf-equiv, and @sde. Neural ODEs and training by simulation are treated by @chen2018node. Three results this chapter leans on are established earlier in the book rather than here: normalising flows and the change-of-variables density in @sec-flows, Tweedie's formula in @sec-ddpm-tweedie, and the probability-flow ODE and its DDIM discretisation in the score-SDE chapter.
